nodes.title: Aims of time series analysis
Time series decomposition
nodes.content:
\textbf{\textcolor{red}{TIME SERIES DECOMPOSITION}}

View $Y_t$ as composed of: a \textbf{Trend}, a \textbf{Seasonal} comp., a \textbf{cycle}, and an \textbf{Erratic} comp.

\textbf{Additive}: $Y_t = T_t + S_t + C_t + E_t$

\textbf{Multiplicative}: $Y_t = T_t \cdot S_t \cdot C_t \cdot E_t$

note $\log$ transforms a multiplicative decomposition into an additive one

\textbf{Diagnostic:} if the seasonal swing grows with the level of the series, prefer the multiplicative form (or model $\log Y_t$ additively).

nodes.title: Fitting a trend
Fitting a seasonal component
nodes.content:
\textbf{\textcolor{red}{FITTING A SEASONAL COMPONENT}}

For $Y_t = S_t + E_t$ (purely seasonal, no trend; assume mean zero, $\bar{y}_t = 0$):

\textbf{1. Seasonal factors.} For monthly data introduce $\alpha_{\text{Jan}}, \alpha_{\text{Feb}}, \dots, \alpha_{\text{Dec}}$ with $\sum_m \alpha_m = 0$:
\[ y_t = \alpha_{\text{month}(t)} + E_t. \]

Note they can always sum to 0, just change the intercept of the model (the level of the trend)

\textbf{2. Moving averages.} For monthly data, $\mathrm{MA}(12)$:
\[ y_t^{\text{deseason.}} = \frac{0.5\, y_{t-6} + y_{t-5} + \dots + y_{t+5} + 0.5\, y_{t+6}}{12}. \]

nodes.title: How to assign the Probability law of the process
nodes.content:
\textbf{\textcolor{red}{HOW TO ASSIGN THE PROBABILITY LAW OF THE PROCESS}}



Defining a \textbf{statistical model} for a stoch.\ process means specifying the joint probability law of $(Y_t)$, i.e.\ specifying \[ P(Y_1, \dots, Y_n) \] for any $n$ and any $t_1, 

Build it up layer by layer.

\textbf{Step 1 — Univariate marginal distributions.} For every $t \in T$ assign the marginal density of $Y_t$:\[ p_t(y), \qquad t \in T. \]E.g.\ ``$Y_t \sim \mathcal{N}(\mu_t, \sigma_t^2)$ for each $t$''. This pins down where each $Y_t$ lives, but says nothing about how different times relate.

\textbf{Step 2 — Bivariate densities (the correlation structure).} For every pair of times $(s, t)$ assign the joint density of $(Y_s, Y_t)$:\[ p_{s,t}(y_s, y_t). \]This captures the \textbf{dependence}: e.g.\ $\mathrm{Cov}(Y_s, Y_t) = 0$ for $s \neq t$ gives an iid process; $\mathrm{Cov}(Y_s, Y_t) = \sigma^2 \rho^{|t-s|}$ gives an AR(1)-like correlation; and so on.

\textbf{Step 3 — Finite-dimensional distributions (FDDs).} Generalise Step 2 to every finite collection of times $(t_1, \dots, t_n)$ — the joint density of $(Y_{t_1}, \dots, Y_{t_n})$:\[ p_{t_1,\dots,t_n}(y_1,\dots,y_n). \]The family $\{p_{t_1,\dots,t_n}\}$ ranging over all $n$ and all index tuples is the \textbf{finite-dimensional distributions} of the process.

\textbf{Result (Kolmogorov extension).} Under \textbf{consistency} conditions (marginals of higher-order FDDs equal the lower-order FDDs, plus permutation invariance), the family of FDDs \emph{uniquely defines} the probability law of the whole process $(Y_t)_{t \in T}$.



\textbf{\textcolor{red}{Why marginals alone are not enough.}} Three processes, all with the \emph{same} marginal $Y_t \sim \mathcal{N}(0,1)$, but totally different joint behaviour:

$\bullet$ \textbf{Process A (iid):} $Y_t \stackrel{\text{iid}}{\sim} \mathcal{N}(0,1)$ — marginal $\mathcal{N}(0,1)$; uncorrelated, jagged noise.

$\bullet$ \textbf{Process B (perfect autocorrelation):} $Y_t \equiv X$ with $X \sim \mathcal{N}(0,1)$ — marginal $\mathcal{N}(0,1)$ (every $Y_t$ is literally the same r.v.); the path is a flat horizontal line at random height $X$.

$\bullet$ \textbf{Process C (AR(1)):} $Y_t = \rho\, Y_{t-1} + \sqrt{1-\rho^2}\,\varepsilon_t$ with $\varepsilon_t \sim \mathcal{N}(0,1)$ and $|\rho|<1$ — marginal $\mathcal{N}(0,1)$ (stationary); smooth wiggle with autocorrelation $\rho^{|t-s|}$.

The picture below confirms: identical marginals (right column), wildly different paths (left column).

nodes.title: Forecasting algorithms — Cases 0, 1, 2 (SES / Holt / Holt-Winters)
nodes.content:
\textbf{\textcolor{red}{FORECASTING ALGORITHMS — CASES 0, 1, 2}}

Predict $y_{t+1}\mid y_{1:t}$ — often the ultimate goal. At time $t$ define the \textbf{forecast function}\[ f_t : \mathbb{N} \to \mathbb{R}, \qquad f_t(h) = \hat y_{t+h\mid t}, \]i.e.\ $f_t(h)$ is the $h$-step-ahead forecast made using information up to $t$.


The formulas belwo actually derive from SSM ! 

\begin{tabular}{|l|l|l|l|}
\hline
 & \textbf{\textcolor{red}{Case 0 (SES)}} \textit{(no trend, no seasonality)} & \textbf{\textcolor{red}{Case 1 — Holt}} \textit{(add trend)} & \textbf{\textcolor{red}{Case 2 — Holt-Winters}} \textit{(add seasonality)} \\
\textbf{Forecast} $\hat y_{t+h\mid t}$ & $\hat y_{t+h\mid t} = L_t$ \;\textit{(flat)} & $\hat y_{t+h\mid t} = L_t + h\, B_t$ \;\textit{(level + slope $\times h$)} & $\hat y_{t+h\mid t} = L_t + h\, B_t + S_{t+h-m}$ \;\textit{(level + slope + seasonal at matching period)} \\
\textbf{State} $L_t$ \textit{(level)} & $L_t = \alpha\, y_t + (1-\alpha)\, L_{t-1}$ & $L_t = \alpha\, y_t + (1-\alpha)\,(L_{t-1} + B_{t-1})$ — \textit{use best yesterday prediction} & $L_t = \alpha\,(y_t - S_{t-m}) + (1-\alpha)\,(L_{t-1} + B_{t-1})$ — \textit{avoid double counting} \\
\textbf{State} $B_t$ \textit{(slope)} & — & $B_t = \beta\,(L_t - L_{t-1}) + (1-\beta)\, B_{t-1}$ — \textit{B is the average change in the last day and in the past} & $B_t = \beta\,(L_t - L_{t-1}) + (1-\beta)\, B_{t-1}$ \\
\textbf{State} $S_t$ \textit{(seasonal)} & — & — & $S_t = \gamma\,(y_t - L_{t-1} - B_{t-1}) + (1-\gamma)\, S_{t-m}$ --- \textit{S is the average of this period's seasonal deviation (today's observation minus the predicted non-seasonal part $L_{t-1} + B_{t-1}$) and the seasonal factor one full cycle ago $S_{t-m}$} \\
\textbf{Recursive form of} $\hat y$ & substitute $\hat y_{t\mid t-1} = L_{t-1}$ into the state update: $\hat y_{t+1\mid t} = \alpha\, y_t + (1-\alpha)\, \hat y_{t\mid t-1}$ & $\hat y_{t+1\mid t} = L_t + B_t = \alpha\, y_t + (1-\alpha)\, \hat y_{t\mid t-1} + B_t$ & $\hat y_{t+1\mid t} = L_t + B_t + S_{t+1-m} = \alpha\, y_t + (1-\alpha)\, \hat y_{t\mid t-1} + B_t + (S_{t+1-m} - S_{t-m})$ \\
\textbf{Forecast-error correction} & $\hat y_{t+1\mid t} = \hat y_{t\mid t-1} + \alpha\,(y_t - \hat y_{t\mid t-1})$ & — & — \\
\hline
\end{tabular}


\textbf{\textcolor{red}{$L_t$ and exponential smoothing.}} The simplest forecast is just a \emph{weighted average of past observations with geometrically decreasing weights} (not a regression --- the weight parameter $\alpha$ is fixed, not estimated): \[ \underbrace{\hat y_{t+1\mid t}}_{L_t} \;=\; \alpha\, y_t \;+\; \underbrace{\alpha(1-\alpha)\, y_{t-1} \;+\; \alpha(1-\alpha)^2\, y_{t-2} \;+\; \dots \;+\; \alpha(1-\alpha)^{t-1}\, y_1}_{(1 - a) \hat y_{t-1\mid t-2 = L_{t-1} } } , \qquad 0 < \alpha < 1, \sum_{k=0}^{t-1} \alpha\,  (1-\alpha)^k \underbrace{=}_{t \to \infty}\; 1.\]

You can always apply this to compute Lt, but it will be correct only in he Case 0

nodes.title: Summaries of a stochastic process
nodes.content:
\textbf{\textcolor{red}{SUMMARIES OF A STOCHASTIC PROCESS}}

For a single random variable $X$, the basic summaries are $\mathbb{E}[X]$ and $\mathrm{Var}(X)$. For a stochastic process $(Y_t)_{t \ge 1}$ these become \emph{functions of time} (and pairs of times):

$\bullet$ \textbf{Mean function}  $\mu : t \mapsto \mu(t) = \mathbb{E}[Y_t],  t = 1, 2, \dots$

$\bullet$ \textbf{Variance function}  $\sigma^2 : t \mapsto \sigma^2(t) = \mathrm{Var}(Y_t),  t = 1, 2, \dots$

$\bullet$ \textbf{Autocovariance function}  $\gamma : (t, t') \mapsto \gamma(t, t') = \mathrm{Cov}(Y_t, Y_{t'}) = \mathbb{E}\!\left[(Y_t - \mu(t))(Y_{t'} - \mu(t'))\right],  t, t' = 1, 2, \dots$

$\bullet$ \textbf{Autocorrelation function}  $\rho : (t, t') \mapsto \rho(t, t') = \dfrac{\gamma(t, t')}{\sqrt{\sigma^2(t)\, \sigma^2(t')}} \in [-1, 1],  t, t' = 1, 2, \dots$

\textit{Consistency check:} $\gamma(t, t) = \sigma^2(t)$ and $\rho(t, t) = 1$.

nodes.title: Stationarity (2nd-order / weak)
nodes.content:
\textbf{\textcolor{red}{STATIONARITY}}

A time series $(Y_t)$ is \textbf{stationary} (2nd-order / weak) if $E(Y_t)$ and $E(Y_t Y_{t+h})$ exist, are finite, and do not depend on $t$, for every $h = 1, 2, \dots$

\[ \mu(t) = \mu  \text{(constant mean)} \]
\[ \sigma^2(t) = \sigma^2  \text{(constant variance)} \]
\[ \gamma(t, t+h) = \tilde\gamma(h)  \text{(autocov.\ depends on lag $h$ only)} \]

nodes.title: Stationarity does not imply strict stat.
nodes.content: Exception: for a Gaussian process the law is fully pinned down by the first two moments, so under Gaussianity weakly stationary $\Rightarrow$ strictly stationary.

nodes.title: Strict stationarity
nodes.content:
\textbf{\textcolor{red}{STRICT STATIONARITY}}

A time series $(Y_t)$ is \textbf{strictly stationary} if the joint distribution of $(Y_t, Y_{t+1}, \dots, Y_{t+h})$ does not depend on $t$, for any $h = 1, 2, \dots$

This implies\[ (Y_{t_1}, \dots, Y_{t_k}) \stackrel{d}{=} (Y_{t_1+h}, \dots, Y_{t_k+h}), \qquad \text{for any } (t_1, \dots, t_k) \text{ and } h, \]
...Obviously: 
In particular, the marginal distribution of $Y_t$ does not depend on $t$, thus\[ Y_1 \stackrel{d}{=} Y_2 \stackrel{d}{=} \cdots \stackrel{d}{=} Y_t \stackrel{d}{=} \cdots \]If $\mathbb{E}(Y_t)$ and $\mathbb{E}(Y_t Y_{t+h})$ exist and are finite, this implies that the mean function and the variance function are constant over time, $\mu(t) = \mu$ and $\sigma^2(t) = \sigma^2$.

Also the bivariate distribution of $(Y_t, Y_{t+h})$ does not depend on $t$, thus\[ (Y_1, Y_{1+h}) \stackrel{d}{=} (Y_2, Y_{2+h}) \stackrel{d}{=} \cdots \stackrel{d}{=} (Y_t, Y_{t+h}) \stackrel{d}{=} \cdots \]This implies that the autocovariance $\gamma(t, t+h)$, which is computed through the density of $(Y_t, Y_{t+h})$, does not depend on $t$ but only on the lag $h$.


\textbf{\textcolor{red}{Warning — what `for every $(t_1,\dots,t_k)$' alone does NOT mean.}} Demanding that the joint law of $(Y_{t_1}, \dots, Y_{t_k})$ be the same \emph{across all choices} of $(t_1,\dots,t_k)$ (dropping the shift quantifier and asking that the law depend on $k$ only, not on the times themselves) is a \textbf{much stronger} condition: it would force, e.g., $\mathrm{Corr}(Y_1, Y_2) = \mathrm{Corr}(Y_1, Y_{100})$, killing any lag-decay correlation structure. An AR(1) with $|\rho|<1$ would fail it.

nodes.title: Most trivial example of stoch. process
nodes.content:
\textbf{\textcolor{red}{MOST TRIVIAL EXAMPLE OF STOCH.\ PROCESS}}

Say $Y_t,\ t \ge 0$ are independent. If, additionally, $Y_t$ have a common distribution (i.i.d.) with $p$:
\[ p_n(y_1,\dots,y_n) = p(y_1)\, p(y_2) \cdots p(y_n) = \prod_{i=1}^n p(y_i). \]

If only indep.\ (not necessarily identically distrib.):
\[ p_n(y_1,\dots,y_n) = p_1(y_1)\, p_2(y_2) \cdots p_n(y_n). \]



Both assume independence: irrealistic for time series

nodes.title: Introducing correlation — full dependence
nodes.content:
\textbf{\textcolor{red}{INTRODUCING CORRELATION (DEPENDENCE)}}

\textbf{Step 1 — Full dependence (general chain rule).}\[ p_n(y_1, \dots, y_n) = p(y_1)\, p(y_2 \mid y_1)\, p(y_3 \mid y_1, y_2) \cdots p(y_n \mid y_1, \dots, y_{n-1}) = p(y_1) \prod_{t=2}^{n} p(y_t \mid y_1, \dots, y_{t-1}). \]This is fully general — no assumption made. The cost is that each conditional $p(y_t \mid y_1, \dots, y_{t-1})$ depends on the \emph{entire} past, so we have $n-1$ growing-dimension conditionals to specify or estimate. Infeasible in practice.

nodes.title: Example 2: categorical time series
nodes.content:
\textbf{\textcolor{red}{EXAMPLE 2 — CATEGORICAL TIME SERIES (PANEL ON VOTE INTENTION)}}

Anderson \& Goodman (1957) — panel study on US vote intention, May–October 1940 (6 monthly interviews). For each individual, $Y_t \in \mathcal{Y} = \{1, 2, 3\}$ with $1 = \text{Republican}$, $2 = \text{Democrat}$, $3 = \text{Don't know}$.

\textbf{Assumption:} $(Y_t)$ is a \textbf{homogeneous Markov chain}, i.e.\ (i) the vote intention $Y_t$ depends on the past only through $Y_{t-1}$ (Markov property), and (ii) the transition probabilities are constant over time.

\textbf{Transition matrix} (given as data for the exercises):

\begin{tabular}{|c|c|c|c|}
\hline
$t-1 \;\backslash\; t$ & $1$ (Rep.) & $2$ (Dem.) & $3$ (Don't know) \\
\hline
$1$ (Rep.)        & $0.6$ & $0.3$ & $0.1$ \\
$2$ (Dem.)        & $0.1$ & $0.7$ & $0.2$ \\
$3$ (Don't know)  & $0.0$ & $0.4$ & $0.6$ \\
\hline
\end{tabular}

\textit{Initial state:} at $t = 0$, the person is undecided, $Y_0 = 3$.

\textbf{\textcolor{red}{Worked exercises}}

\textbf{(a) Probability that at $t = 1$ she expresses a preference for the Democrat Party.}\[ P(Y_1 = 2 \mid Y_0 = 3) = p_{3,2} = 0.4. \]
\textbf{(b) Probability that at $t = 1$ she is still undecided and at $t = 2$ she expresses a preference for the Democrat Party.}\[ P(Y_1 = 3,\ Y_2 = 2 \mid Y_0 = 3) = P(Y_1 = 3 \mid Y_0 = 3)\, P(Y_2 = 2 \mid Y_1 = 3) = p_{3,3}\, p_{3,2} = 0.6 \times 0.4 = 0.24. \]

\textbf{(c) Probability that she expresses a preference for the Democrat Party at $t = 2$.}\[ P(Y_2 = 2 \mid Y_0 = 3) = \sum_{k=1}^{3} P(Y_2 = 2 \mid Y_1 = k)\, P(Y_1 = k \mid Y_0 = 3) = \sum_{k=1}^{3} p_{k,2}\, p_{3,k} = 0.52. \]
\textbf{(d) Given that she expresses a preference for the Democrat Party at $t = 2$, probability that she was still undecided at $t = 1$.}

\emph{Generic rule.} For any events $A$ and $B$ (with $P(B) > 0$),\[ P(A \mid B) = \frac{P(A \cap B)}{P(B)}. \]Basically: the probability that $A$ and $B$ happen together, given that $B$ has happened.

With an extra event $C$ held fixed in the background the same rule reads\[ P(A \mid B,\, C) = \frac{P(A \cap B \mid C)}{P(B \mid C)}. \]

\emph{In our case:} take $A = \{Y_1 = 3\}$, $B = \{Y_2 = 2\}$, $C = \{Y_0 = 3\}$. Then\[ P\bigl(\underbrace{Y_1 = 3}_{A} \,\big|\, \underbrace{Y_2 = 2}_{B},\ \underbrace{Y_0 = 3}_{C}\bigr) = \frac{P\bigl(\underbrace{Y_1 = 3,\ Y_2 = 2}_{A \cap B} \mid \underbrace{Y_0 = 3}_{C}\bigr)}{P\bigl(\underbrace{Y_2 = 2}_{B} \mid \underbrace{Y_0 = 3}_{C}\bigr)}. \]

The numerator is exactly exercise (b) ($= 0.24$) and the denominator is exactly exercise (c) ($= 0.52$), so\[ P(Y_1 = 3 \mid Y_2 = 2,\ Y_0 = 3) = \frac{0.24}{0.52} \approx 0.4615. \]

\textbf{(e1) Full probability distribution of $Y_2$, given $Y_0 = 3$.}

Apply the law of total probability conditioning on $Y_1$ and use the Markov property:\[ P(Y_2 = j \mid Y_0 = 3) = \sum_{k=1}^{3} P(Y_2 = j \mid Y_1 = k)\, P(Y_1 = k \mid Y_0 = 3) = \sum_{k=1}^{3} p_{k,j}\, p_{3,k}. \]Compute each entry:

$\bullet$ $P(Y_2 = 1 \mid Y_0 = 3) = p_{1,1} p_{3,1} + p_{2,1} p_{3,2} + p_{3,1} p_{3,3} = 0.6 \cdot 0 + 0.1 \cdot 0.4 + 0 \cdot 0.6 = 0.04$.

$\bullet$ $P(Y_2 = 2 \mid Y_0 = 3) = p_{1,2} p_{3,1} + p_{2,2} p_{3,2} + p_{3,2} p_{3,3} = 0.3 \cdot 0 + 0.7 \cdot 0.4 + 0.4 \cdot 0.6 = 0.52$  (same as (c)).

$\bullet$ $P(Y_2 = 3 \mid Y_0 = 3) = p_{1,3} p_{3,1} + p_{2,3} p_{3,2} + p_{3,3} p_{3,3} = 0.1 \cdot 0 + 0.2 \cdot 0.4 + 0.6 \cdot 0.6 = 0.44$.

Write it as a row vector,\[ \boldsymbol\pi_2 := (P(Y_2 = 1 \mid Y_0 = 3),\ P(Y_2 = 2 \mid Y_0 = 3),\ P(Y_2 = 3 \mid Y_0 = 3)) = (0.04,\ 0.52,\ 0.44). \]

\textbf{(e2) Full probability distribution of $Y_3$, given $Y_0 = 3$.}

Apply the same idea one step further out — condition on $Y_2$ and use the Markov property — but now plug in the distribution of $Y_2$ we just got in (e1):\[ P(Y_3 = l \mid Y_0 = 3) = \sum_{k=1}^{3} P(Y_3 = l \mid Y_2 = k)\, P(Y_2 = k \mid Y_0 = 3) = \sum_{k=1}^{3} p_{k,l}\, \boldsymbol\pi_2(k). \]

In our case,\[ \boldsymbol\pi_3 = \boldsymbol\pi_2\, \mathbf{P} = (0.04,\ 0.52,\ 0.44) \begin{pmatrix} 0.6 & 0.3 & 0.1 \\ 0.1 & 0.7 & 0.2 \\ 0.0 & 0.4 & 0.6 \end{pmatrix} = (0.076,\ 0.552,\ 0.372). \]So $P(Y_3 = 1 \mid Y_0 = 3) = 0.076$, $P(Y_3 = 2 \mid Y_0 = 3) = 0.552$, $P(Y_3 = 3 \mid Y_0 = 3) = 0.372$ — and they sum to $1$.

nodes.title: Example 3: Simple random walk
nodes.content:
\textbf{\textcolor{red}{EXAMPLE 3 — SIMPLE RANDOM WALK}}

\textbf{Setting.} A player starts with capital $y_0 > 0$. At each step the player gets a gain of $+1$ with probability $p$, or a loss of $-1$ (i.e.\ gain $-1$) with probability $1-p$. Let $Y_t$ denote the capital at step $t$. The process $(Y_t)_{t \ge 0}$ is called a \textbf{simple random walk}.

\textbf{Decomposition.} Let $Z_t$ be the random gain at step $t$. The $Z_t$ are i.i.d.\ with\[ Z_t \stackrel{\text{iid}}{\sim} \begin{cases} +1 & \text{with probability } p, \\ -1 & \text{with probability } 1-p. \end{cases} \]Then $Y_t$ satisfies the recursion\[ Y_t = Y_{t-1} + Z_t = y_0 + Z_1 + Z_2 + \dots + Z_t = y_0 + \sum_{i=1}^{t} Z_i, \qquad t = 1, 2, \dots \]

\textbf{Markov property.} The recursion $Y_t = Y_{t-1} + Z_t$ would not be enough on its own — in general $Z_t$ could depend on the past $Y_0, \dots, Y_{t-1}$. Using the assumption that the $Z_t$ are i.i.d.\ and independent of the past $Y$'s, we get the Markov property:\[ P(Y_t = y \mid Y_0 = y_0, Y_1 = y_1, \dots, Y_{t-1} = i) = P(Y_t = y \mid Y_{t-1} = i) = \begin{cases} p & \text{if } y = i + 1, \\ 1-p & \text{if } y = i - 1, \\ 0 & \text{otherwise.} \end{cases} \]In words: the conditional distribution of $Y_t$ given the entire past depends only on the value $Y_{t-1} = i$ — not on how the player reached $i$.

\textbf{Generalisation (gain not restricted to $\pm 1$).} If the $Z_t$ are i.i.d.\ with finite mean $\mathbb{E}(Z_t) = \mu$ and variance $\mathrm{Var}(Z_t) = \sigma^2$, and $Y_0 = y_0$, the same recursion gives\[ Y_t = y_0 + \sum_{i=1}^{t} Z_i, \qquad t = 1, 2, \dots, \]and $(Y_t)$ is called a (general) \textbf{random walk}. Applications: in physics, $Y_t$ is the position of a particle. In finance, $Y_t$ is the log-price of an asset under a perfect-market assumption — the log-price at $t$ equals the previous log-price plus an unpredictable gain $Z_t$.

\textbf{Non-stationarity.} Take, for simplicity, $y_0 = 0$ and $\mathbb{E}(Z_t) = 0$. Then\[ \mathbb{E}(Y_t) = \sum_{i=1}^{t} \mathbb{E}(Z_i) = 0, \qquad \mathrm{Var}(Y_t) = \sum_{i=1}^{t} \mathrm{Var}(Z_i) \underbrace{=}_{iid} t\, \sigma^2. \]The variance grows linearly in $t$ — \textbf{not constant} — so the random walk is \emph{not} (weakly) stationary.

bronian motion: take this random walk, with very small steps, in rapid succession; in the limits, this processes appears as a continous motion.

nodes.title: Example 4: Random walk with drift
nodes.content:
\textbf{\textcolor{red}{EXAMPLE 4 — RANDOM WALK WITH DRIFT (ASYMMETRIC GAINS / PROBABILITIES)}}

\textbf{Setting.} Same recursion as the simple random walk of Example 3,\[ Y_t = Y_{t-1} + Z_t = y_0 + \sum_{i=1}^{t} Z_i, \qquad t = 1, 2, \dots, \]but now the increments $Z_t$ are i.i.d.\ with non-zero mean. The number\[ \mu = \mathbb{E}[Z_t] \neq 0 \]is called the \textbf{drift} of the random walk; $\sigma^2 = \mathrm{Var}(Z_t)$ is the per-step variance.

\textbf{Where asymmetry can come from.}

$\bullet$ \textbf{Asymmetric probabilities, $\pm 1$ payoffs:} $Z_t = +1$ w.p.\ $p$, $-1$ w.p.\ $1-p$, with $p \neq 1/2$. Then $\mu = 2p - 1$, $\sigma^2 = 4 p (1-p)$. Still called a \emph{simple} random walk.

$\bullet$ \textbf{Asymmetric payoffs:} $Z_t = +a$ w.p.\ $1/2$, $-b$ w.p.\ $1/2$, with $a \neq b$. Then $\mu = (a-b)/2$, $\sigma^2 = (a+b)^2/4$. No longer \emph{simple} (steps not in $\{-1, +1\}$), but still a random walk.

$\bullet$ \textbf{General i.i.d.\ increments:} any law for $Z_t$ with finite mean $\mu$ and variance $\sigma^2$.

\textbf{Markov property holds.} Because the $Z_t$ are i.i.d.\ and independent of the past $Y$'s, $P(Y_t \in \cdot \mid Y_0, \dots, Y_{t-1}) = P(Y_t \in \cdot \mid Y_{t-1})$ — exactly as in Example 3. Asymmetry does not break the Markov structure; it just shifts the conditional mean.

\textbf{Trend + zero-mean walk decomposition (for all cases above).} Write\[ Y_t = \underbrace{(y_0 + t\, \mu)}_{\text{deterministic trend}} \;+\; \underbrace{\sum_{i=1}^{t} (Z_i - \mu)}_{\text{zero-mean random walk}}. \]So a random walk with drift is just a line of slope $\mu$ through $y_0$, plus a zero-mean random walk fluctuating around it.

\textbf{Non-stationarity (generalisation).} With $Y_0 = y_0$, $\mathbb{E}[Z_t] = \mu$, and $\mathrm{Var}(Z_t) = \sigma^2$,\[ \mathbb{E}[Y_t] = y_0 + \sum_{i=1}^{t} \mathbb{E}[Z_i] = y_0 + t\, \mu, \qquad \mathrm{Var}(Y_t) = \sum_{i=1}^{t} \mathrm{Var}(Z_i) = t\, \sigma^2. \]A random walk with drift is \textbf{not stationary}.

nodes.title: Ergodic properties of a Markov chain (Theorem 2.1)
nodes.content:
\textbf{\textcolor{red}{ERGODIC PROPERTIES OF A MARKOV CHAIN}}

In general the random variables $Y_n$ are \emph{not} identically distributed — the distribution of $Y_n$ varies with $n$, hence the process $(Y_t)_{t \ge 0}$ is not (strictly) stationary. We want to study its \textbf{asymptotic behaviour} as $n \to \infty$.

\textbf{Question.} Does the conditional distribution of $Y_n$ given the initial state $Y_0 = j$,\[ P(Y_n = k \mid Y_0 = j), \qquad k = 1, \dots, N, \]converge to some limit distribution $p^*(\cdot)$? And is this limit independent of the starting state $j$? If so, the Markov chain is called \textbf{ergodic} — intuitively, the initial state becomes irrelevant for large $n$.

\textbf{\textcolor{red}{Theorem 2.1.}} Let $(Y_t)$ be an \textbf{irreducible} and \textbf{aperiodic} Markov chain with finite state space $\mathcal{Y} = \{1, \dots, N\}$. Then:

\textbf{(1)} The conditional distribution $P(Y_n = \cdot \mid Y_0 = j)$ converges to a limit distribution $p^*(\cdot)$, independent of $j$:\[ \lim_{n \to \infty} P(Y_n = k \mid Y_0 = j) = p^*(k) > 0, \qquad \forall j, k \in \mathcal{Y}, \qquad \sum_{k \in \mathcal{Y}} p^*(k) = 1. \]

\textbf{(2)} The limit $p^*$ satisfies the fixed-point equation\[ \underbrace{p^*(k)}_{\text{prob.\ of being in } k \text{ (next step)}} \;=\; \sum_{i \in \mathcal{Y}} \underbrace{p^*(i)}_{\text{prob.\ of being in } i \text{ (current step)}} \cdot \underbrace{p_{i,k}}_{\text{transition } i \to k}, \qquad \forall k \in \mathcal{Y}. \]In row-vector form: $\boldsymbol{p}^* = \boldsymbol{p}^* \, \mathbf{P}$.

\textit{Two readings of the same sum.}

\textbf{(a) Always-true one-step update (law of total probability).} For \emph{any} sequence of distributions $\boldsymbol\pi_n$ produced by the chain,\[ \underbrace{\boldsymbol\pi_{n+1}(k)}_{\text{next-step prob.}} \;=\; \sum_{i \in \mathcal{Y}} \underbrace{\boldsymbol\pi_n(i)}_{\text{current prob.}} \cdot \underbrace{p_{i,k}}_{\text{transition } i \to k}, \]i.e.\ $\boldsymbol\pi_{n+1} = \boldsymbol\pi_n\, \mathbf{P}$. This is just LTP: ``sum the ways to arrive in $k$''. It is \textbf{always true}, for every $\boldsymbol\pi_n$ and every $\mathbf{P}$.

\textbf{(b) Fixed-point (stationarity) equation.} Set $\boldsymbol\pi_{n+1} = \boldsymbol\pi_n = \boldsymbol p$ in (a) — i.e.\ ask which distributions stay unchanged after one step:\[ \underbrace{p(k)}_{\text{same on both sides}} \;=\; \sum_{i \in \mathcal{Y}} p(i)\, p_{i,k}, \qquad \text{i.e.\ } \boldsymbol p = \boldsymbol p\, \mathbf{P}. \]
**So basically we are saying, you apply transition porbabilitis, you trasform to the next state, but the marginal probability is the same as t-1.**

This is a \textbf{constraint}: it is \emph{not} satisfied by most distributions. The set of distributions for which it holds is exactly the set of \textbf{stationary / invariant} distributions of the chain — fixed points of the one-step map $\boldsymbol\pi \mapsto \boldsymbol\pi\, \mathbf{P}$.

Note that since the limit distribution is stationary, we can also prove its uniqueness (we're not jumpting aroudn at the limit!). 


\emph{Concrete check (2-state chain $\mathbf{P} = (\begin{smallmatrix} 0.8 & 0.2 \\ 0.4 & 0.6 \end{smallmatrix}))$.} Take $\boldsymbol\pi = (0.5,\,0.5)$: applying (a), $\boldsymbol\pi\,\mathbf{P} = (0.6,\,0.4) \neq \boldsymbol\pi$ — so it is \emph{not} a fixed point. Take instead $\boldsymbol p^* = (2/3,\,1/3)$: $\boldsymbol p^*\,\mathbf{P} = (2/3,\,1/3) = \boldsymbol p^*$ — fixed point, hence stationary. Theorem 2.1 part (2) says the limit $p^*$ is a fixed point of $\mathbf{P}$.


\textbf{\textcolor{red}{In words.}} Theorem 2.1 means that, at the limit, $Y_n$ is distributed according to the discrete law\[ Y_n \;\stackrel{d}{\to}\; \begin{cases} 1 & \text{with probability } p^*(1), \\ 2 & \text{with probability } p^*(2), \\ \;\vdots & \;\vdots \\ N & \text{with probability } p^*(N), \end{cases} \]i.e.\ $Y_n$ becomes (approximately, for large $n$) a categorical random variable on $\{1, \dots, N\}$ with probabilities $p^*(1), p^*(2), \dots, p^*(N)$ — regardless of the starting state $Y_0$.



\textit{Remark.} If $P(Y_n = k \mid Y_0 = j) \to p^*(k)$ independently of $j$, then the marginal $P(Y_n = k)$ converges to the same limit! Hence, it is enough to study the asymptotic behaviour of the conditional distribution $P(Y_n = k \mid Y_0 = j)$ — results for the marginal $P(Y_n = k)$ then follow automatically.

nodes.title: Conditions of Theorem 2.1 — recurrent / aperiodic / irreducible
nodes.content:
\textbf{\textcolor{red}{CONDITIONS OF THEOREM 2.1 — RECURRENT, APERIODIC, IRREDUCIBLE}}

Fix a state $j$ and consider the Markov chain started at $Y_0 = j$. Let\[ f_j \;=\; P(\text{the chain ever returns to state } j \mid Y_0 = j). \]

\textbf{Recurrence / transience.}

$\bullet$ If $f_j = 0$: a return to $j$ is impossible.

$\bullet$ If $f_j = 1$: the chain certainly visits $j$ again — state $j$ is \textbf{recurrent}.

$\bullet$ If $f_j < 1$: state $j$ is \textbf{transient}.

$\bullet$ State $j$ is \textbf{recurrent non-null} if $f_j = 1$ (P(i is visited infinitely often) = 1 ) \emph{and} the mean recurrence time (expected number of steps to return to $j$) is finite.

\textbf{Periodicity.} State $j$ is \textbf{periodic with period $t$} if a return to $j$ is possible only at $t, 2t, 3t, \dots$ steps. If no such $t > 1$ exists, $j$ is \textbf{aperiodic}.

\textbf{Closed set / irreducibility.} A set $C \subseteq \mathcal{Y}$ is \textbf{closed} if no one-step transition is possible from any state inside $C$ to any state outside $C$, i.e.\ \[ p_{j,k} = 0  \text{whenever } j \in C \text{ and } k \notin C. \]A Markov chain is \textbf{irreducible} if there are no (proper) closed sets — equivalently, every state is reachable from every other state in finitely many steps.

\emph{Example (reducible chain).} On $\mathcal{Y} = \{1, 2, 3, 4\}$,\[ \mathbf{P} = \begin{pmatrix} 1/3 & 0 & 2/3 & 0 \\ 0 & 1/4 & 0 & 3/4 \\ 1/2 & 0 & 1/2 & 0 \\ 0 & 1/2 & 0 & 1/2 \end{pmatrix} \]is reducible: the two sets $C_1 = \{1, 3\}$ and $C_2 = \{2, 4\}$ are each closed (no row in $C_1$ has positive mass on a column in $C_2$, and vice versa).

See how there can be no common limit distribution for any starting point! 

\textbf{Consequences for an irreducible chain.}

$\bullet$ All states belong to the same class: either all recurrent, or all transient. How can it be that half are recurrent half transient if every state is reachable from every other state in finitely many steps? 

$\bullet$ If the state space is \emph{finite}, at least one state is visited infinitely often (so is recurrent non-null); combined with irreducibility, \emph{all} states are recurrent non-null. This means that the probability in 1) of Th 2.1 is positive

$\bullet$  Recurrent states could still be periodic, but Theorem 2.1 excludes that case by assumption.

nodes.title: Example 5: Random walk + noise (state-space)
nodes.content:
\textbf{\textcolor{red}{EXAMPLE 5 — RANDOM WALK + NOISE  (LOCAL-LEVEL MODEL)}}

A simple \textbf{state-space model} with two layers: a \emph{latent} random walk $x_t$ that we cannot observe directly, and an \emph{observed} series $y_t$ that equals $x_t$ plus independent measurement noise.

\textbf{State equation (latent).}\[ x_t = x_{t-1} + z_t, \qquad z_t \stackrel{\text{iid}}{\sim} \mathcal{N}(0,\ \sigma_z^2), \qquad x_0 \text{ given}. \]This is a Gaussian random walk on the hidden state $x_t$. $z_t$ is the \emph{signal (process) noise}.

\textbf{Observation equation.}\[ y_t = x_t + \varepsilon_t, \qquad \varepsilon_t \stackrel{\text{iid}}{\sim} \mathcal{N}(0,\ \sigma_\varepsilon^2), \qquad \{\varepsilon_t\} \perp \{z_s\}. \]$y_t$ is the noisy version of $x_t$ we actually see. The two noise streams $(z_t)$ and $(\varepsilon_t)$ are independent of each other and of $x_0$. $\varepsilon_t$ is the \emph{measurement noise}.

\textbf{What this captures.}

$\bullet$ \textbf{Why $x_t$ is \emph{smooth} and $y_t$ is \emph{noisy}.} Unrolling the state equation,\[ \begin{aligned} x_1 &= x_0 + z_1, \\ x_2 &= x_1 + z_2 = x_0 + z_1 + z_2, \\ x_3 &= x_2 + z_3 = x_0 + z_1 + z_2 + z_3, \\ &\;\vdots \\ x_t &= x_0 + z_1 + z_2 + \dots + z_t, \end{aligned} \]so $x_t$ is an \textbf{integrator} of the $z$'s: every past shock $z_1, \dots, z_{t-1}$ is still living inside $x_t$ (each gets carried forward through $x_{t-1}$). Neighbours therefore differ by exactly \emph{one} fresh shock,\[ x_t - x_{t-1} = z_t, \qquad \mathrm{Var}(x_t - x_{t-1}) = \sigma_z^2, \]so the curve drifts persistently with small step-to-step changes — that's the smooth look.

The observation does \emph{not} integrate $\varepsilon_t$: each $\varepsilon_t$ appears only in $y_t$ and is gone next step (no memory of past observation errors). Hence two neighbouring $y$'s differ by \emph{three} independent shocks,\[ y_t - y_{t-1} = z_t + \varepsilon_t - \varepsilon_{t-1}, \qquad \mathrm{Var}(y_t - y_{t-1}) = \sigma_z^2 + 2\sigma_\varepsilon^2, \]so $y_t$ is jittered by a fresh, non-persistent kick at every step — that's the noisy look. Same i.i.d.\ Gaussian shocks on both sides; what differs is that $z_t$ feeds an integrator (memory), while $\varepsilon_t$ is added pointwise (no memory).

$\bullet$ The two variance parameters set the \emph{signal-to-noise ratio} $\sigma_z^2 / \sigma_\varepsilon^2$ (the true variance of the process). You want to know what is xt to predict yt, so you want to estimate how its errors are distirbuted!

$\bullet$ Limit $\sigma_z^2 \to 0$: $x_t$ is essentially constant and $y_t$ becomes iid noise around it.

$\bullet$ Limit $\sigma_\varepsilon^2 \to 0$: $y_t \approx x_t$ — we see the latent walk directly.

\textbf{Markov structure.} The state $x_t$ is Markov, and the observation depends only on the current state:\[ p(x_t \mid x_{1:t-1}, y_{1:t-1}) = p(x_t \mid x_{t-1}), \qquad p(y_t \mid x_{1:t}, y_{1:t-1}) = p(y_t \mid x_t). \]Conditionally on $x_0$, the joint process $((x_t, y_t))_{t \ge 1}$ is Gaussian.

\textbf{Moments.} Taking $x_0 = 0$ for simplicity,\[ \mathbb{E}[x_t] = 0, \qquad \mathrm{Var}(x_t) = t\, \sigma_z^2, \]\[ \mathbb{E}[y_t] = 0, \qquad \mathrm{Var}(y_t) = t\, \sigma_z^2 + \sigma_\varepsilon^2. \]Both processes are \textbf{not stationary}: $\mathrm{Var}(x_t)$ grows linearly in $t$, and $y_t$ inherits the growth plus a constant noise floor $\sigma_\varepsilon^2$.

\textbf{Why it matters.} This is the prototype of the \textbf{state-space} (or \emph{dynamic linear}) model. Given only $y_{1:t}$, the natural problem is to estimate the latent $x_t$: \textbf{filtering} (estimate $x_t$ from $y_{1:t}$), \textbf{smoothing} (from $y_{1:T}$), \textbf{prediction} (estimate $x_{t+h}$ from $y_{1:t}$). The Kalman filter handles all three in closed form because both equations are linear and Gaussian.

\emph{Picture below:} one realization of the latent $x_t$ (smooth dark curve) and the observed $y_t$ (dots scattering around it). The light band is $x_t \pm \sigma_\varepsilon$ — the typical magnitude of the measurement noise.

nodes.title: tuning alfa in SES
nodes.content:
In SES: 
$\bullet$ if $\alpha \approx 1$: $\hat{y}_{t+1\mid t} \approx y_t$ (follows the data)

$\bullet$ if $\alpha \approx 0$: $\hat{y}_{t+1\mid t} \approx$ constant

\textbf{\textcolor{red}{Choosing $\alpha$ — grid search.}} Try a grid $\alpha \in \{0.01, 0.02, \dots, 0.99\}$. For each $\alpha$, compute the one-step-ahead forecasts on held-out data and evaluate one of:

\textbf{MAE} (Mean Absolute Error):\[ \mathrm{MAE} = \frac{1}{n} \sum_{t=1}^{n} \left| y_t - \hat{y}_t \right| \]

\textbf{MSE} (Mean Squared Error):\[ \mathrm{MSE} = \frac{1}{n} \sum_{t=1}^{n} \left( y_t - \hat{y}_t \right)^2 \]

\textbf{MAPE} (Mean Absolute Percentage Error):\[ \mathrm{MAPE} = \frac{100\%}{n} \sum_{t=1}^{n} \left| \frac{y_t - \hat{y}_t}{y_t} \right| \]

Pick $\hat\alpha = \arg\min_\alpha \mathrm{(MAE\, /\, MSE\, /\, MAPE)}$. MAE is robust to outliers, MSE penalises large errors more heavily, MAPE is scale-free but blows up when $y_t \approx 0$.

nodes.title: Example 2. White noise
Markov Property
nodes.content:
\textbf{\textcolor{red}{MARKOV PROPERTY}}

\textbf{Definition.} A discrete-time stochastic process $(Y_t)_{t \ge 0}$ with $Y_t \in \mathcal{Y}$ is a \textbf{Markov process} if

$\bullet$ $Y_0 \sim p_0(\cdot)$  (initial distribution), and

$\bullet$ for every $t \ge 1$, $Y_t$ depends on the past observations only through $Y_{t-1}$:\[ p(y_t \mid y_0, y_1, \dots, y_{t-1}) = p(y_t \mid y_{t-1}). \]

\textbf{Joint density} Plugging the Markov property into the general chain rule collapses the joint to one-step transitions only:\[ p_n(y_0, y_1, \dots, y_n) = p_0(y_0) \prod_{t=1}^{n} p(y_t \mid y_{t-1}). \]
Note the set $\mathcal{Y}$ of possible values of $Y_t$ is called the \textbf{state space} of the Markov chain.

So the law of the process is fully specified by

$\bullet$ the \textbf{initial distribution} $p_0(\cdot)$ of $Y_0$;

$\bullet$ the family of \textbf{one-step transition kernels} $\{p(y_t \mid y_{t-1}) : t \ge 1\}$.


\textbf{\textcolor{red}{Conditional independence statement.}} The Markov property is equivalent to saying that, for every $t \ge 1$, \[ Y_t \;\perp\!\!\!\perp\; (Y_0, Y_1, \dots, Y_{t-2}) \;\big|\; Y_{t-1}, \]i.e.\ given the immediate past $Y_{t-1}$, the current value $Y_t$ is conditionally independent of everything earlier.

\textbf{\textcolor{red}{DAG view.}} A Markov chain is naturally drawn as a directed acyclic graph (DAG):\[ Y_0 \to Y_1 \to Y_2 \to \dots \to Y_{t-1} \to Y_t \to \dots \]\emph{Reading the DAG:} if you remove the node $Y_{t-1}$, the node $Y_t$ becomes disconnected from $(Y_0, \dots, Y_{t-2})$. Graphically, $Y_{t-1}$ d-separates $Y_t$ from its earlier ancestors — exactly the conditional-independence statement above.



\textbf{\textcolor{red}{TRANSITION MATRIX}}

Finite state space $\mathcal{Y} = \{1, 2, \dots, N\}$. The transition probabilities at time $t$ are\[ p^{(t)}_{i,j} = P(Y_t = j \mid Y_{t-1} = i), \qquad i, j \in \mathcal{Y}. \]Arrange them in a matrix $\mathbf{P}^{(t)}$ with \emph{rows} indexed by the state at $t-1$ and \emph{columns} indexed by the state at $t$:

\begin{tabular}{|c|c|c|c|c|}
\hline
$t - 1 \;\backslash\; t$ & $1$ & $2$ & $\cdots$ & $N$ \\
\hline
$1$ & $p^{(t)}_{1,1}$ & $p^{(t)}_{1,2}$ & $\cdots$ & $p^{(t)}_{1,N}$ \\
$2$ & $p^{(t)}_{2,1}$ & $p^{(t)}_{2,2}$ & $\cdots$ & $p^{(t)}_{2,N}$ \\
$\vdots$ & $\vdots$ & $\vdots$ & $\ddots$ & $\vdots$ \\
$N$ & $p^{(t)}_{N,1}$ & $p^{(t)}_{N,2}$ & $\cdots$ & $p^{(t)}_{N,N}$ \\
\hline
\end{tabular}

\textbf{Row-stochastic:} each row sums to 1, $\sum_{j=1}^{N} p^{(t)}_{i,j} = 1$ for every $i$ and every $t$ — given that you are in state $i$ at $t-1$, you must end up \emph{somewhere} at time $t$.

\textbf{Homogeneous case.} If the transition probabilities do not depend on $t$, i.e.\ $p^{(t)}_{i,j} = p_{i,j}$ for every $t$, then the chain is \textbf{homogeneous}. The superscript drops:\[ \mathbf{P}^{(t)} \equiv \mathbf{P} = \big(p_{i,j}\big)_{i,j \in \mathcal{Y}}, \]a single $N \times N$ matrix that — together with the initial distribution $p_0(\cdot)$ — fully specifies the law of the chain.

nodes.title: Markov Property, continuous case
nodes.content:
\textbf{\textcolor{red}{MARKOV PROPERTY — CONTINUOUS CASE}} \emph{(discrete time, continuous state space)}

So far the state space has been finite ($\mathcal{Y} = \{1, \dots, N\}$), which is well suited to categorical time series. In general $\mathcal{Y}$ can be countable ($\mathcal{Y} = \{1, 2, \dots\}$) or continuous, e.g.\ $\mathcal{Y} = (-\infty, +\infty)$. In the continuous case the law of the Markov chain is specified by densities rather than by a matrix of probabilities:

$\bullet$ \textbf{Initial density:}  $Y_0 \sim f_0(\cdot)$.

$\bullet$ \textbf{Transition densities:}  $Y_t \mid Y_{t-1} = y_{t-1} \;\sim\; f_t(\,\cdot \mid y_{t-1})$, for every $t \ge 1$.

\textbf{Joint density.} By the Markov property combined with the chain rule, the joint density of $(Y_0, \dots, Y_n)$ collapses to one-step transitions:\[ f_n(y_0, y_1, \dots, y_n) \;=\; f_0(y_0)\, f_1(y_1 \mid y_0)\, f_2(y_2 \mid y_1) \cdots f_n(y_n \mid y_{n-1}). \]

\textbf{Example (AR(1)).} A discrete-time, continuous-state Markov process given by\[ Y_t = \varphi\, Y_{t-1} + \varepsilon_t, \qquad \varepsilon_t \stackrel{\text{iid}}{\sim} \mathcal{N}(0, \sigma^2), \qquad t \ge 1, \]with $Y_0$ given.  If $\varphi = 1$, $(Y_t)$ is a \emph{random walk} (Example 3).

\textbf{\textcolor{red}{INFERENCE FOR MARKOV CHAINS}} \emph{(panel of i.i.d.\ chains)}

\textbf{Setting.} When a Markov chain is used as a statistical model, the transition probabilities $p_{i,j}$ are unknown and must be estimated from data. 

Causality: see if transition probabilities chnage after treatment 
Prediction: infer the transition probabilities to predict future values. 

Two data designs:

$\bullet$ \emph{Single long path:} we observe one trajectory $(Y_0, Y_1, \dots, Y_T)$ for $T$ large; estimate $p_{i,j}$ from time averages.

$\bullet$ \emph{Panel:} we observe $n$ short trajectories $(Y_{k,0}, \dots, Y_{k,T})$, $k = 1, \dots, n$, one per individual. This is the Anderson \& Goodman (1957) setting; we focus on this case. In other words, we have a random sample of markov chains characterized by the same transition matrices! 

\textbf{Modelling assumptions.}

\textbf{(M1)} Each individual time series $(Y_{k,t})_{t \ge 0}$ is a \emph{homogeneous} Markov chain with transition matrix $\mathbf{P}$. Recall no statistical mdoel is true... the point is if the model is "reasonable". 

\textbf{(M2)} The $n$ trajectories are i.i.d.\ across individuals: $(Y_{k,t})_{t \ge 0} \stackrel{\text{iid}}{\sim}$ Markov chain with transition matrix $\mathbf{P}$, $k = 1, \dots, n$. So independente: No spillovers + Identical distribution (the marginals are all the same, notice this is different from saying the marginals are time invariant (homogeneous)) = no individaul effects here. 

\textit{Caveats one may want to relax:} higher-order Markov (memory $r > 1$); non-homogeneity ($\mathbf{P}_t$ depends on $t$); individual-specific transition matrices (heterogeneity).

nodes.title: Proof: the counts ratio is the MLE
nodes.content:
Proof: The counts ratio is the MLE



\textbf{\textcolor{red}{Proof — the counts ratio is the MLE.}}

\emph{Step 1: define the likelihood.} The \textbf{likelihood} is the probability of observing the data we actually saw, written as a function of the unknown parameter. Here the parameter is the transition matrix $\theta = \mathbf{P} = (p_{i,j})$:\[ L(\mathbf{P};\, \text{data}) \;=\; \mathbb{P}\bigl(\text{data} \,\big|\, \mathbf{P}\bigr), \qquad \text{viewed as a function of } \mathbf{P}. \]

\emph{Step 2: factorise.} Condition on the fixed initial values $y_{k,0}$. Using (M2) i.i.d.\ trajectories, (M1) Markov property + chain rule, and homogeneity (so each one-step conditional is $p_{y_{k,t-1},\, y_{k,t}}$):\[ L(\mathbf{P};\, \underbrace{y_1, \dots, y_n)}_{\text{data from N indiv. eacn observed T times}} \;=\; \underbrace{\prod_{k=1}^{n}\,}_{\text{k individuals}} \underbrace{p_{y_{k,0}, y_{k,1}}\,}_{\text{whatever state the individaul visits}} p_{y_{k,1}, y_{k,2}} \cdots p_{y_{k,T-1}, y_{k,T}}. \]

\emph{Step 3: regroup by transition counts.} The same factor $p_{i,j}$ appears in the product once per observed transition $i \to j$ in the panel (obivously, just grouping probabilities!):\[ L(\mathbf{P};\, \text{data}) \;=\; \prod_{i=1}^{M}\prod_{j=1}^{M} \underbrace{p_{i,j}^{\, n_{i,j}}}_{g(T(x), \theta))}. \] So the statistic $T(x) = \{n_{i,j}\}$ is \textbf{jointly sufficient} for $\mathbf{P}$ 

\emph{Step 4: find MLE by maximise L wrt $p_{i,j}$ and you get: \[ \boxed{\hat p_{i,j} \;=\; \frac{n_{i,j}}{n_{i,+}}, \qquad i, j = 1, \dots, M.} \]

We study the behaviour of $\hat p_{i,j}$ as $n \to \infty$ under the assumption\[ \frac{n_h(0)}{n} \;\longrightarrow\; \eta_h, \qquad h = 1, \dots, M. \]Recall that the MLE of the $i$-th row of $\mathbf{P}$ is $(\hat p_{i,1}, \dots, \hat p_{i,M})$ with $\hat p_{i,j} = n_{i,j}/n_{i,+}$, and\[ (n_{i,1}, \dots, n_{i,M}) \;\sim\; \mathrm{Multinomial}(n_{i,+};\ p_{i,1}, \dots, p_{i,M}). \]Note: $n_{i,+}$ is itself random, since it depends on how often the panel visits state $i$.

$\hat p_{ij}$ is just a ratio, by CLT is multivariate gaussian. It says: average of many independent identically-distributed things is approximately Gaussian, with mean = true mean of one draw, variance = (variance of one draw)/(number of draws).


\textit{Step 1 --- handle the randomness of $n_{i,+}$.} Define\[ \varphi_i \;=\; \sum_{h=1}^{M} \eta_h \sum_{t=1}^{T} p^{(t-1)}_{h,\, i}, \]where $p^{(t-1)}_{h, i}$ is the probability of state $i$ at time $t-1$ given state $h$ at time $0$. So $n\, \varphi_i$ is the expected total number of observations in state $i$ over $t = 0, 1, \dots, T-1$, averaged over the initial distribution. Then\[ \frac{n_{i,+}}{n} \;\longrightarrow\; \varphi_i  \text{as } n \to \infty, \qquad \text{so } n_{i,+} \approx n\, \varphi_i. \]

\textit{Step 2}. Conditional on $n_{i,+}$ known, standard multinomial-MLE theory gives, for $j, h = 1, \dots, M$, $j \neq h$,\[ \mathbb{E}(\hat p_{i,j}) = p_{i,j}, \qquad \mathrm{Var}(\hat p_{i,j}) = \frac{p_{i,j}(1 - p_{i,j})}{n_{i,+}}, \qquad \mathrm{Cov}(\hat p_{i,j},\ \hat p_{i,h}) = -\frac{p_{i,j}\, p_{i,h}}{n_{i,+}}, \]and an asymptotic multivariate Gaussian distribution for $(\hat p_{i,1}, \dots, \hat p_{i,M})$.


\textit{Result.} The rows of $\hat{\mathbf{P}}$ are \textbf{asymptotically independent} (each multinomial, the joint stays multinomial), and the $i$-th row is approximately multivariate Gaussian:\[ (\hat p_{i,1}, \dots, \hat p_{i,M})^\top \;\approx\; \mathcal{N}_M\bigl(p_i,\ \Sigma_i\bigr), \]
\textit{Approximated variances (plug-in).} The unknowns $p_{i,j}$ and $\varphi_i$ are replaced by consistent estimators: $\hat p_{i,j}$ for $p_{i,j}$, and (using $n_{i,+} \approx n\,\varphi_i$) just the observed row total $n_{i,+}$ in the denominator. This gives the practical estimator\[ \widehat{\mathrm{Var}}(\hat p_{i,j}) \;=\; \frac{\hat p_{i,j}\,(1 - \hat p_{i,j})}{n_{i,+}}, \qquad \widehat{\mathrm{Cov}}(\hat p_{i,j},\, \hat p_{i,h}) \;=\; -\frac{\hat p_{i,j}\,\hat p_{i,h}}{n_{i,+}} (j \neq h). \]

\textit{Asymptotic confidence intervals.} A level-$(1-\alpha)$ CI for $p_{i,j}$ is\[ \boxed{\;\hat p_{i,j} \;\pm\; z_{\alpha/2}\,\sqrt{\frac{\hat p_{i,j}\,(1 - \hat p_{i,j})}{n_{i,+}}}\;} \]with $z_{\alpha/2}$ the $(1-\alpha/2)$-quantile of $\mathcal{N}(0,1)$ (e.g.\ $z_{0.025} \approx 1.96$ for $95\%$).

nodes.title: Hidden Markov  Models
nodes.content:
\textbf{\textcolor{red}{HIDDEN MARKOV MODELS (HMM)}}

An HMM is a discrete time stochastic process  $$(\underbrace{Y_t}_{\text{time series}}, \underbrace{S_t}_{\text{stochastic process}})$$ where the distribution that generates the observation $Y_t$ depends on the state of an underlying \emph{unobserved} process $(S_t)$ called state process.

\emph{When is it useful?} ARMA-type models assume stationarity. HMMs are tailored for \emph{non-stationary} series with change points / regime switches — e.g.\ speech recognition, business-cycle detection, unbounded-count series (Poisson observation "number of calls in one hour"  ) where the rate switches between states. Why not modelign it with a poisson? becasse poisson is st mean and variance coincide (do not want this constraint)

\textbf{\textcolor{red}{Toy 3-regime Gaussian HMM.}} A simple example with three regimes is\[ Y_t = \begin{cases} \mu_1 + e_t & \text{if } S_t = 1, \\ \mu_2 + e_t & \text{if } S_t = 2, \\ \mu_3 + e_t & \text{if } S_t = 3, \end{cases} \qquad e_t \stackrel{\text{iid}}{\sim} \mathcal{N}(0, \sigma^2). \]More compactly, $Y_t = \mu_{S_t} + e_t$.

\textbf{\textcolor{red}{The "equation" of the hidden chain (3-regime example).}} For this toy example, $K = 3$ and the state space is $\mathcal{S} = \{1, 2, 3\}$. The conditional law of $S_t$ given $S_{t-1} = i$ is the categorical distribution given by row $i$ of $\mathbf{P}$:
\[ S_t \mid S_{t-1} = i \;\sim\; \text{Categorical}\bigl(p_{i,1},\, p_{i,2},\, p_{i,3}\bigr), \]
i.e.\ $P(S_t = j \mid S_{t-1} = i) = p_{i,j}$, plus the initial law $S_0 \sim \pi = (\pi_1, \pi_2, \pi_3)$. This is the "equation" of the hidden Markov chain --- once you draw $S_t$ from this categorical, the observation is $Y_t = \mu_{S_t} + e_t$.

\textit{Note:} the observed process $(Y_t)$ itself is generally \emph{not} Markov — observing $Y_{t-1}$ does not pin down $S_{t-1}$. The Markov property lives at the level of the \emph{hidden} chain.

\textbf{\textcolor{red}{Formal definition.}} There exists a \emph{latent} state process $(S_t)_{t \ge 0}$ that is a homogeneous Markov chain on a finite state space $\mathcal{S} = \{1, \dots, M\}$ with initial distribution $\pi$ and transition matrix $\mathbf{P} = (p_{i,j})$, $p_{i,j} = P(S_t = j \mid S_{t-1} = i)$, such that:

$\bullet$ \textbf{Markov property of the hidden chain:}\[ p(s_t \mid s_{0:t-1}, y_{1:t-1}) \;=\; p(s_t \mid s_{t-1}) \;=\; p_{s_{t-1}, s_t}. \]

$\bullet$ \textbf{Conditional independence of the observations:} given the latent path, the $Y_t$'s are independent and $Y_t$ depends only on $S_t$, hence, for any set E \[ p(y_t \in E \mid s_{0:t}, y_{1:t-1}) \;=\; p(y_t \in E \mid s_t). \] Recall St is never observed. Big idea! once you have st you do not need anythign else!

\textbf{\textcolor{red}{Specifying the law of an HMM.}} It follows that the probability law of the hidden Markov process $\bigl((S_t, Y_t)\bigr)_{t \ge 0}$ is specified by assigning:

$\bullet$ the \textbf{initial distribution} of the hidden state: $S_0 \sim \pi$ on $\mathcal{S} = \{1, \dots, M\}$, that is $(p_0(1), ... , p_0(k))$; 

$\bullet$ the \textbf{transition matrix} of the hidden chain: $A = \mathbf{P} = (p_{i,j})_{i,j \in \mathcal{S}}$ with $p_{i,j} = P(S_t = j \mid S_{t-1} = i)$;

$\bullet$ the \textbf{emission distributions} $\{p(y \mid s) : s \in \mathcal{S}\}$, one per state

\textbf{\textcolor{red}{DAG view of an HMM — reading conditional independence.}}
