nodes.title: Example emission matrices
nodes.content:
\textbf{\textcolor{red}{EXAMPLE EMISSION MATRICES}}

Recall the emission distributions are the probability distribution of the observable variable $Y_t$ given the state $S_t = j$, for $j = 1, \dots, K$. Two standard cases.

\textbf{\textcolor{red}{1. Discrete (non-parametric) case.}} Suppose $Y_t$ takes values in the finite set $\{1, \dots, M\}$. The general (non-parametric) form of the emission distribution in state $j$ is

\[ Y_t \mid S_t = j \;\sim\; \bigl(\, \underbrace{P(Y_t = 1 \mid S_t = j)}_{b_{j,1}}, \;\dots,\; \underbrace{P(Y_t = i \mid S_t = j)}_{b_{j,i}}, \;\dots,\; \underbrace{P(Y_t = M \mid S_t = j)}_{b_{j,M}} \,\bigr), \]

i.e.\ we let $P(Y_t = y \mid S_t = j) \equiv b_{j,y}$, $y = 1, \dots, M$. Collecting the emission probabilities $b_{j,y}$ in the \emph{emission matrix}

\[ B = [b_{j,y}]_{j=1,\dots,K;\; y=1,\dots,M}, \]

we use the compact notation $\phi = (A, B, \pi)$ to represent the HMM. Specification of the HMM then requires choosing the number of states $K$ and the probability matrices $A$, $B$ and the initial vector $\pi$.

\textbf{\textcolor{red}{2. Parametric case --- Poisson emissions.}} In other cases one may want a parametric emission distribution, so that $Y_t \mid S_t = j \sim p(\,\cdot \mid \theta_j^*)$, $j = 1, \dots, K$. For example, for the earthquakes data (unbounded counts), one could assume
\[ Y_t \mid (S_t = j) \;\sim\; \text{Poisson}(\theta_j^*), \]
that is, at state $j$, $Y_t$ has a Poisson distribution with parameter $\theta_j^*$. 

\textbf{\textcolor{red}{Why this fixes the plain-Poisson defects.}} A single Poisson forces (i) mean $=$ variance, (ii) no serial dependence, (iii) one mode. Letting the rate \emph{switch} with a Markov chain breaks all three:

$\bullet$ \textbf{Different mean and variance per regime.} Within state $j$, both equal $\lambda_j^*$, but across regimes they differ --- a "quiet" state has small mean \emph{and} small variance, an "active" one has large mean \emph{and} large variance.

$\bullet$ \textbf{Autocorrelation.} Sticky regimes ($p_{j,j}$ near $1$) mean neighbouring $Y_t$'s likely share the same rate, so
\[ \text{Cov}(Y_t, Y_{t+h}) \;=\; \text{Cov}(\lambda_{S_t}^*, \lambda_{S_{t+h}}^*) \;>\; 0. \]
No additive $\epsilon$ needed --- the dependence comes from persistence of the hidden chain.

nodes.title: Specification
nodes.content:
\textbf{\textcolor{red}{1. MODEL SPECIFICATION}}

Choosing the number $K$ of hidden states is a natural first question. In some applications, $K$ is suggested by knowledge of the domain under study. In other cases, one can try a few different values of $K$ and compare the performance of the resulting models.

nodes.title: Estimation
nodes.content:
\textbf{\textcolor{red}{2. ESTIMATION OF THE UNKNOWN PARAMETERS}}

We can estimate the unknown parameters of an HMM by maximum likelihood. The first step is to write the expression of the likelihood. Let us focus on the \emph{discrete non-parametric case}, where $Y_t \in \{1, \dots, M\}$, and the HMM is characterized by the unknown parameters are $\phi = (A, B, \pi)$).

The likelihood of $\phi$ is the joint probability of the observed sequence $y_1, \dots, y_T$, read as a function of $\phi$; that is,

\[ \begin{aligned} L(\phi \mid y_{1:T}) &\;=\; P(Y_1 = y_1, \dots, Y_T = y_T \mid \phi) \\ &\;=\; \sum_{(s_0, \dots, s_T) \,\in\, \{1, \dots, K\}^{T+1}} \underbrace{P(Y_{1:T} = y_{1:T},\, S_{0:T} = s_{0:T} \mid \phi)}_{\text{joint of obs.\ and states}} \\ &\;=\; \sum_{(s_0, \dots, s_T) \,\in\, \{1, \dots, K\}^{T+1}} \underbrace{P(S_0 = s_0 \mid \phi)}_{\text{all initials } \pi_{s_0}} \;\cdot\; \underbrace{\prod_{t=1}^{T} p_{s_{t-1}, s_t}}_{\text{all possible transitions}} \;\cdot\; \underbrace{\prod_{t=1}^{T} b_{s_t, y_t}}_{\text{all possible emissions}} \end{aligned} \]

Over all possible values of the hidden state sequence $(s_0, s_1, \dots, s_T)$. Each $s_t$ can be any state in $\{1, 2, \dots, K\}$, independently in the sum. So the sum runs over all tuples of length $T + 1$ with entries in $\{1, \dots, K\}$ --- i.e.\ $K^{T+1}$ tuples.

\emph{Tiny example.} $K = 2$, $T = 2$. Then $s_{0:2}$ can be any of
\[ (1,1,1),\; (1,1,2),\; (1,2,1),\; (1,2,2),\; (2,1,1),\; (2,1,2),\; (2,2,1),\; (2,2,2), \]
i.e.\ $2^3 = 8$ sequences. The sum $\sum_{s_{0:2}}$ adds the term once per sequence.





A direct evaluation of such joint probability may be involved, because the temporal dependence of the process $(Y_t)$ may be complex. Concretely, you need to compute: 
\[ P(Y_{1:T} = y_{1:T} \mid \phi) \;=\; \sum_{s_{0:T} \in \{1, \dots, K\}^{T+1}} \pi_{s_0}\, p_{s_0, s_1}\, b_{s_1, y_1}\, \cdots\, p_{s_{T-1}, s_T}\, b_{s_T, y_T}. \]
That is $K^{T+1}$ terms --- \emph{exponential} in $T$. With $K = 3$ and $T = 100$ that is $\sim 10^{48}$ summands. \emph{That} is what "involved" means.

\textbf{\textcolor{red}{Step 1 --- Likelihood by basic probability laws.}} Start from the definition and marginalise the hidden path:
\[ L(\phi \mid y_1, \dots, y_T) \;=\; \sum_{(s_0, \dots, s_T) \,\in\, \{1, \dots, K\}^{T+1}} \underbrace{P(Y_{1:T} = y_{1:T} \mid S_{0:T} = s_{0:T}, \phi)}_{A} \;\cdot\; \underbrace{P(S_{0:T} = s_{0:T} \mid \phi)}_{B}. \]
We now compute $A$ and $B$ separately.

\textbf{\textcolor{red}{Computing $A$.}} By \emph{Assumption 2} (conditional independence of the observations given the latent path, with each $Y_t$ depending only on $S_t$),
\[ A \;=\; P(Y_1 = y_1, \dots, Y_T = y_T \mid S_0 = s_0, \dots, S_T = s_T, \phi) \;\underbrace{=}_{\text{assumption 2}}\; \prod_{t=1}^{T} P(Y_t = y_t \mid S_t = s_t, \phi) \;=\; b_{s_1, y_1}\, b_{s_2, y_2}\, \cdots\, b_{s_T, y_T}. \]

\textbf{\textcolor{red}{Computing $B$.}} By the chain rule and the Markov property of the hidden chain,
\[ \begin{aligned} B \;=\; P(S_0 = s_0, \dots, S_T = s_T \mid \phi) &= P(S_0 = s_0 \mid \phi)\, P(S_1 = s_1 \mid S_0 = s_0, \phi) \cdots \\ & \cdots P(S_T = s_T \mid S_{T-1} = s_{T-1}, \phi) \\ &= \pi_{s_0}\, p_{s_0, s_1}\, \cdots\, p_{s_{T-1}, s_T}. \end{aligned} \]

\textbf{\textcolor{red}{Putting it together.}} Multiplying $A$ and $B$ and summing over all possible state sequences $s_{0:T}$,
\[ L(\phi \mid y_1, \dots, y_T) \;=\; \sum_{(s_0, \dots, s_T) \,\in\, \{1, \dots, K\}^{T+1}} A \cdot B \;=\; \sum_{(s_0, \dots, s_T) \,\in\, \{1, \dots, K\}^{T+1}} \pi_{s_0}\, p_{s_0, s_1}\, b_{s_1, y_1}\, p_{s_1, s_2}\, b_{s_2, y_2}\, \cdots\, p_{s_{T-1}, s_T}\, b_{s_T, y_T}.  (2) \]


\textbf{\textcolor{red}{Maximisation.}} Once we have the likelihood $L(\phi \mid y_{1:T})$, the MLE $\hat\phi$ is the value that maximises it.

nodes.title: Decoding
nodes.content:
\textbf{\textcolor{red}{3. DECODING}}

In HMMs, decoding means finding the "optimal" state sequence associated with the given observation sequence; in other words, estimating the state sequence $s_{1:T}$ given the data $y_{1:T}$. For simplicity, we consider $s_0$ as fixed, and the parameters $\phi$ as known (or replaced by their MLEs).

There are different optimality criteria.

\textbf{\textcolor{red}{Local criterion.}} For each $t = 1, \dots, T$, choose the state $s_t^*$ which is marginally most likely at time $t$; more precisely, which maximises
\[ \gamma_t(s) \;\equiv\; P(S_t = s \mid y_{1:T}, \phi) \]
with respect to $s \in \{1, \dots, K\}$. This gives the (marginally) optimal state $s_t^* = \arg\max_s \gamma_t(s)$. Repeating for $t = 1, \dots, T$, we get a sequence $\{s_1^*, \dots, s_T^*\}$ of locally optimal states.

\emph{Issue.} When the HMM has state transitions with zero probability (i.e.\ $p_{i,j} = 0$ for some $i, j$), the obtained sequence $s_{1:T}^*$ may in fact be a non-valid sequence (if a transition from $s_t^*$ to $s_{t+1}^*$ is impossible).

\textbf{\textcolor{red}{Global criterion --- Viterbi.}} Find the best path $(\hat s_0, \dots, \hat s_T)$ that maximises the joint conditional probability
\[ \max_{s_{0:T}} P(S_0 = s_0, \dots, S_T = s_T \mid Y_1 = y_1, \dots, Y_T = y_T, \phi). \]

This conditional probability can be computed using Bayes theorem. However, we can more easily exploit the computations already carried out for the MLE. Notice that
\[ \begin{aligned} & P(S_0 = s_0, \dots, S_T = s_T,\, Y_1 = y_1, \dots, Y_T = y_T \mid \phi) \\ & \underbrace{=}_{\text{chain rule}} P(S_0 = s_0, \dots, S_T = s_T \mid Y_1 = y_1, \dots, Y_T = y_T, \phi)\, P(Y_1 = y_1, \dots, Y_T = y_T \mid \phi), \end{aligned} \]
where the latter factor on the right-hand side does not depend on $s_{0:T}$. Therefore, maximising the conditional joint probability with respect to $s_{0:T}$ is equivalent to maximising the joint probability $P(S_0 = s_0, \dots, S_T = s_T,\, Y_1 = y_1, \dots, Y_T = y_T \mid \phi)$, which we have computed already. Now we need to optimize by $S_{0:T}$!

nodes.title: Example — Nile river
nodes.content:
\textbf{\textcolor{red}{EXAMPLE --- Nile river data}}

In LAB 2 we consider a few examples on the use of HMMs with R, using the R package \texttt{depmixS4}.

The following example considers the \emph{Nile river data}, available in R, which provides the measurements of the annual flow of the Nile river in the period 1871--1970. We envisage a change point around the year 1898, when the construction of the first dam in Aswan was started. This suggests to fit an HMM with $K = 2$ states --- so $(S_t)_{t \ge 0}$ is a Markov chain with state space $\mathcal{S} = \{1, 2\}$ --- and to assume a \emph{Gaussian emission distribution} with state-specific parameters:
\[ \begin{aligned} Y_t \mid S_t = 1 &\;\sim\; \mathcal{N}(\mu_1^*, \sigma_1^*), \\ Y_t \mid S_t = 2 &\;\sim\; \mathcal{N}(\mu_2^*, \sigma_2^*), \end{aligned} \]
where the (unknown) parameters are $\theta_1^* = (\mu_1^*, \sigma_1^*)$ and $\theta_2^* = (\mu_2^*, \sigma_2^*)$. We also fix the initial distribution as
\[ \pi \;=\; \bigl(\, \pi_1 = 0, \;\; \pi_2 = 1 \,\bigr). \]

\textbf{\textcolor{red}{The "equation" of the hidden chain.}} For this 2-state chain, the conditional law of $S_t$ given $S_{t-1} = i$ is the categorical distribution given by row $i$ of $\mathbf{P}$:
\[ S_t \mid S_{t-1} = i \;\sim\; \text{Categorical}\bigl(p_{i,1}, p_{i,2}, \dots, p_{i,K}\bigr), \]
i.e.\ $P(S_t = j \mid S_{t-1} = i) = p_{i,j}$, plus the initial law $S_0 \sim \pi$. This is the "equation" of a Markov chain.





\textbf{\textcolor{red}{MLE of the transition matrix.}} The maximum likelihood estimates of the transition matrix, provided by \texttt{depmixS4}, are
\begin{tabular}{c|cc} $t-1 \backslash t$ & $1$ & $2$ \\ \hline $1$ & $1.00$ & $0.00$ \\ $2$ & $0.04$ & $0.97$ \end{tabular}

\textbf{\textcolor{red}{MLE of the emission parameters.}} The MLEs of the parameters $\theta_j^*$ are
\[ \hat\theta_1^* = (\hat\mu_1^*, \hat\sigma_1^*) = (850.57,\; 124.45), \qquad \hat\theta_2^* = (\hat\mu_2^*, \hat\sigma_2^*) = (1097.15,\; 133.75). \]

\emph{Remark.} Reporting the MLEs is not enough. One should also provide the \textbf{standard errors} of the MLEs (possibly approximated by bootstrap techniques), or at least their \emph{asymptotic} standard errors, obtained from the asymptotic properties of MLEs. The computation of the standard errors for the MLEs of the fitted HMM, using the R package \texttt{depmixS4}, is illustrated in Lab 2.

nodes.title: Exercise — weather/activity filtering
nodes.content:
\textbf{\textcolor{red}{EXERCISE --- Filtering: weather $\to$ activity}}

\textbf{Setup.} A person's daily activity depends on the weather, which is hidden. We observe only the activity.

$\bullet$ Hidden state space: $\mathcal{S} = \{1 = \text{sunny},\, 2 = \text{rainy}\}$ ($K = 2$).

$\bullet$ Observation space: $\mathcal{Y} = \{1 = \text{walk},\, 2 = \text{shop},\, 3 = \text{clean}\}$ ($M = 3$).

\textbf{Initial distribution} $\pi$: $P(S_1 = \text{sunny}) = 0.6$, $P(S_1 = \text{rainy}) = 0.4$.

\textbf{Transition matrix} $A$ (rows = state at $t-1$, columns = state at $t$):
\begin{tabular}{c|cc} $t-1 \backslash t$ & sunny & rainy \\ \hline sunny & $0.7$ & $0.3$ \\ rainy & $0.4$ & $0.6$ \end{tabular}

\textbf{Emission matrix} $B$ (rows = state, columns = activity):
\begin{tabular}{c|ccc} $S_t \backslash Y_t$ & walk & shop & clean \\ \hline sunny & $0.6$ & $0.3$ & $0.1$ \\ rainy & $0.1$ & $0.4$ & $0.5$ \end{tabular}


\textbf{\textcolor{red}{(a) After observing $y_1 = \text{walk}$.}}

\emph{What I want.} The unnormalised "score" for each weather state at $t = 1$ given the observation:
\[ \alpha_1(j) \;:=\; P(S_1 = j,\; y_1 = \text{walk}). \]
\emph{Stream of thought.} I have a prior $\pi_j$ on the weather (before observing anything) and an emission $b_{j, \text{walk}}$ saying how compatible "walk" is with weather $j$. By Bayes' rule, the joint is just their product:
\[ \alpha_1(j) \;=\; \underbrace{\pi_j}_{\text{prior on weather}} \;\cdot\; \underbrace{b_{j, \text{walk}}}_{\text{compatibility with "walk"}}. \]
Plug in numbers:
\[ \begin{aligned} \alpha_1(\text{sunny}) &= 0.6 \times 0.6 = 0.36, \\ \alpha_1(\text{rainy}) &= 0.4 \times 0.1 = 0.04. \end{aligned} \]
\emph{Intuition.} Walking is much more compatible with sunny than with rainy ($0.6$ vs $0.1$), so the score for sunny dwarfs the score for rainy --- after seeing "walk", we strongly believe sunny.

\textbf{\textcolor{red}{(b) After also observing $y_2 = \text{shop}$.}}

\emph{What I want.} Same kind of score, now incorporating both observations:
\[ \alpha_2(j) \;:=\; P(S_2 = j,\; y_1 = \text{walk},\; y_2 = \text{shop}). \]
\emph{Stream of thought.} I cannot just look at $y_2$ in isolation: $y_1$ informs $S_1$, $S_1$ informs $S_2$ via the transitions in $A$, so $y_1$ indirectly informs $S_2$. The recipe has \textbf{two moves}.

\textbf{Move 1 --- carry the old belief forward through time.} Push $\alpha_1$ through the transition matrix to get a "predictive score" for $S_2$ given the history $y_1$:
\[ \text{pred}_2(j) \;:=\; \sum_{i \in \mathcal{S}} \alpha_1(i) \cdot p_{i,j} \;=\; P(S_2 = j,\; y_1 = \text{walk}). \]
This is just: "if I was probably-sunny yesterday, where am I likely to be today?" --- weighted by how the chain transitions. SO from y1 we deduced s1 and we use it now. 

\[ \begin{aligned} \text{pred}_2(\text{sunny}) &= 0.36 \times 0.7 + 0.04 \times 0.4 \;=\; 0.252 + 0.016 \;=\; 0.268, \\ \text{pred}_2(\text{rainy}) &= 0.36 \times 0.3 + 0.04 \times 0.6 \;=\; 0.108 + 0.024 \;=\; 0.132. \end{aligned} \]

\textbf{Move 2 --- weight by today's evidence.} Multiply by $b_{j, \text{shop}}$, the compatibility between weather $j$ and the new observation "shop":
\[ \alpha_2(j) \;=\; \underbrace{\text{pred}_2(j)}_{\text{belief from past}} \;\cdot\; \underbrace{b_{j, \text{shop}}}_{\text{compatibility with "shop"}}. \]
\[ \begin{aligned} \alpha_2(\text{sunny}) &= 0.268 \times 0.3 \;=\; 0.0804, \\ \alpha_2(\text{rainy}) &= 0.132 \times 0.4 \;=\; 0.0528. \end{aligned} \]
\emph{Intuition.} The previous "almost certainly sunny" belief is dragged toward rainy because shopping is slightly more compatible with rainy ($0.4$ vs $0.3$). But the pull is mild: sunny stays ahead because the chain is sticky (once sunny, likely still sunny: $p_{\text{sunny}, \text{sunny}} = 0.7$). Net effect: the score ratio drops from $9{:}1$ at $t = 1$ to roughly $1.5{:}1$ at $t = 2$.

\textbf{\textcolor{red}{The recipe in one line.}} For every new observation $y_t$:
\[ \alpha_t(j) \;=\; \underbrace{b_{j, y_t}}_{\text{today's evidence}} \;\cdot\; \underbrace{\sum_{i} \alpha_{t-1}(i) \cdot p_{i,j}}_{\text{yesterday's belief, transitioned}}. \]
That is the entire \emph{forward algorithm}: \emph{transition the old belief, then weight by the new observation}. Repeat at every time step. The numbers $\alpha_t(j) = P(S_t = j,\, y_{1:t})$ accumulate everything you have learned so far about state $j$ and the data jointly.

\textbf{\textcolor{red}{Take-aways.}}

$\bullet$ At each step you do two things: (1) \emph{push the old belief through $A$} to get the prior for today, (2) \emph{multiply by the emission} for today's observation.

$\bullet$ You never throw away the past: $y_1$'s influence on $S_2$ enters through $\alpha_1$ being transitioned forward.

$\bullet$ The $\alpha_t(j)$'s are joint probabilities $P(S_t = j,\, y_{1:t})$, not posteriors. Their relative magnitudes already tell you which state is more likely; summing them gives the data likelihood $P(y_{1:t})$ for free.

nodes.title: State space models (SSM)
nodes.content:
\textbf{\textcolor{red}{STATE SPACE MODELS (SSM)}}

\textbf{\textcolor{red}{One-line intuition.}}  A latent process $(\theta_t)$ evolves Markovianly in its state space, and each observation $Y_t$ is drawn from a distribution determined only by the current state.

So the time series you see is the output of a dynamic system  (the latent procss) + some random disturbances. What is nice is that the underlying dynamic system can have a trends, seasonal componetns, regressive components etc so there is a lot of flesibilty. On top of this they have a very nice probabilityic structure (embed in everything you are doing). 




\textbf{Definition.} A state space model is a pair of processes
\[ \bigl(\, \underbrace{Y_t}_{\text{observation}},\; \underbrace{\theta_t}_{\text{latent}} \,\bigr)_{t \ge 1},  \text{starting at } \theta_0, \]
such that:

$\bullet$ \textbf{(1) Latent Markov state process.} $(\theta_t)_{t \ge 0}$ is a Markov process with continuous state space $\Theta \subseteq \mathbb{R}^p$. (In HMM we had a discrete state space $\mathcal{S} = \{1, \dots, K\}$; here $\Theta$ is continuous.)

$\bullet$ \textbf{(2) Conditional independence of the observations.} Given the latent path $(\theta_t)_{t \ge 0}$, the $Y_t$'s are conditionally independent and each $Y_t$ depends only on $\theta_t$.

\textbf{Equivalently,} the law of an SSM is fully specified by:
\[ \theta_0 \;\sim\; \pi, \qquad \theta_t \mid \theta_{t-1} \;\sim\; p(\theta_t \mid \theta_{t-1}), \qquad Y_t \mid \theta_t \;\sim\; p(y_t \mid \theta_t), \]
i.e.\ an initial law on the state, a transition kernel for the state, and an emission kernel for the observation.



\textbf{\textcolor{red}{Two layers of inference: don't confuse them.}}

The transition kernel $p(\theta_t \mid \theta_{t-1})$ plays \emph{two different roles}, depending on which question you are asking.

$\bullet$ \textbf{(A) Model ingredient (input).} When the model is fully known, $p(\theta_t \mid \theta_{t-1})$ is \emph{given}. You use it \emph{inside} the algorithms (it's the engine of the recursive Bayes update: "carry yesterday's belief forward through the transition"), but it is not the \emph{target} of inference. The four canonical inference tasks --- filtering, smoothing, prediction, decoding --- all assume the model is known and use the transition kernel as an ingredient.

$\bullet$ \textbf{(B) Unknown parameter (target).} When the model has unknown parameters $\phi$, the transition becomes $p(\theta_t \mid \theta_{t-1}; \phi)$ and you genuinely want to learn it from data. In HMMs, $\phi$ contains the entire matrix $\mathbf{P} = (p_{i,j})$. This is a \emph{separate} inference question:

- \emph{Observed Markov chain:} count transitions, $\hat p_{i,j} = n_{i,j} / n_{i,+}$ (the panel-survey exercises).
- \emph{Hidden Markov chain (HMM):} the chain is unobserved, so counting is not possible. Use MLE. \emph{Workflow.} Parameter inference first ($\hat\phi$ from the data), then plug $\hat\phi$ in and do state inference. The four canonical tasks live in the second layer; the transition kernel is itself a \emph{target} only when you're in the first layer.

\textbf{\textcolor{red}{Specialisations / next topics.}}

$\bullet$ The four canonical inference tasks --- \emph{filtering} $p(\theta_t \mid y_{1:t})$, \emph{smoothing} $p(\theta_t \mid y_{1:T})$ , \emph{prediction} $p(\theta_{t+h}, Y_{t+h} \mid y_{1:t})$ --- all use only the joint factorisation above. The Kalman filter, forward algorithm, Viterbi and particle filter are just \emph{efficient ways to do the recursive Bayes update} on that joint.

Note Smoothing for HMM: applies the "local" criterion. For HMM we used viterbi, the global criterion (so smoothign is more or less decoding).

nodes.title: Example SSMs
nodes.content:
\textbf{\textcolor{red}{EXAMPLE SSMs --- Hierarchy of specialisations}}

We progressively add assumptions to the \emph{general SSM} and see which models pop out.

\textbf{\textcolor{red}{The specialisation tree.}}
\[ \underbrace{\text{General SSM}}_{\text{any } p(\theta_t \mid \theta_{t-1}),\, p(y_t \mid \theta_t)} \;\;\xrightarrow[\text{noise Gaussian}]{\text{transition + emission linear}}\;\; \underbrace{\text{DLM}}_{Y_t = F_t \theta_t + v_t,\;\theta_t = G_t \theta_{t-1} + w_t} \begin{cases} \underbrace{\text{Local level}}_{F=G=1,\;p=1} & \text{(RW + noise)} \\ \underbrace{\text{AR(1)}}_{G=\phi,\;F=1,\;V_t=0} & \text{(degenerate)} \\ \underbrace{\text{AR(p)}}_{\text{state} = (Y_t, \dots, Y_{t-p+1})} & \text{(state augmented)} \end{cases} \]
Plus a separate branch:
\[ \text{General SSM} \;\;\xrightarrow[\text{state space} = \{1,\dots,K\}]{\text{discretise the state}}\;\; \underbrace{\text{HMM}}_{S_t \text{ discrete},\; Y_t \mid S_t \sim p(\cdot \mid \theta_{S_t}^*)} . \]

\textbf{\textcolor{red}{(0) General SSM.}} The whole framework lives here. In full generality the transition $p(\theta_t \mid \theta_{t-1})$ and emission $p(y_t \mid \theta_t)$ can be \emph{anything}: discrete, non-linear, non-Gaussian. This is too unwieldy for inference without further structure.

\textbf{\textcolor{red}{(I) DLM = linear Gaussian SSM.}} Assume the dynamics are \emph{linear} and the noise is \emph{Gaussian}:
\[ \theta_t = G_t \theta_{t-1} + w_t, \qquad Y_t = F_t \theta_t + v_t, \qquad w_t \overset{\text{iid}}{\sim} \mathcal{N}(0, W_t),\; v_t \overset{\text{iid}}{\sim} \mathcal{N}(0, V_t), \]
with $G_t \in \mathbb{R}^{p \times p}$ and $F_t \in \mathbb{R}^{m \times p}$ known. \emph{Why this restriction?} The joint of $(\theta_{0:T}, Y_{1:T})$ becomes jointly Gaussian, and all conditionals stay Gaussian --- the recursive Bayes update has a \emph{closed form} (the \emph{Kalman filter}). No Monte Carlo needed.

\textbf{(I.a) Local-level model --- the simplest 1-dim DLM.} Further set $p = m = 1$ and $G_t = F_t = 1$:
\[ \theta_t = \theta_{t-1} + w_t, \qquad Y_t = \theta_t + \varepsilon_t, \qquad w_t \overset{\text{iid}}{\sim} \mathcal{N}(0, \sigma_w^2),\; \varepsilon_t \overset{\text{iid}}{\sim} \mathcal{N}(0, \sigma^2). \]
\emph{This is the random walk + noise model.} Canonical "tracking a noisy quantity" --- e.g.\ a slowly drifting sensor reading. $F_t = 1$ says "observation = state + noise"; $G_t = 1$ says "state evolves as a pure random walk".

\textbf{(I.b) AR(1) as a degenerate DLM.} Take $p = m = 1$, $G_t = \phi$, $F_t = 1$, and \emph{zero observation noise} $V_t = 0$. With state $\theta_t := Y_t$:
\[ \theta_t = \phi\, \theta_{t-1} + \varepsilon_t, \qquad Y_t = \theta_t. \]
The "latent" state isn't really hidden ($Y_t$ reveals it exactly), but formally it satisfies the SSM template. So AR(1) fits as a degenerate DLM.

\textbf{(I.c) AR(p) as a DLM via state augmentation.} 


\textbf{\textcolor{red}{Mini-example: AR(2).}} The full step-by-step matrix multiplication of $G$ and $F$ is in the \emph{AR(2) as SSM --- worked example} snippet (linked). More attached there.

\textbf{\textcolor{red}{(II) HMM = discrete-state SSM.}} A different branch of specialisation: keep the SSM skeleton, but discretise the state.
\[ \theta_t = S_t \in \{1, \dots, K\}, \qquad S_t \mid S_{t-1} = i \sim \text{Categorical}(p_{i,1}, \dots, p_{i,K}), \qquad Y_t \mid S_t = j \sim p(\cdot \mid \theta_j^*). \]
The transition kernel becomes a $K \times K$ matrix $\mathbf{P}$. The emission can be any conditional law (Categorical for non-parametric, Poisson / Gaussian for parametric).

\textbf{\textcolor{red}{Summary table.}}
\begin{tabular}{l|l|l|l} Model & State $\theta_t$ & Transition & Emission \\ \hline General SSM & any & any $p(\theta_t \mid \theta_{t-1})$ & any $p(y_t \mid \theta_t)$ \\ DLM & $\mathbb{R}^p$ & linear Gaussian & linear Gaussian \\ Local level & $\mathbb{R}$ & $\theta_{t-1} + w_t$ & $\theta_t + \varepsilon_t$ \\ AR(1) & $\mathbb{R}$ ($=Y_t$) & $\phi\theta_{t-1} + \varepsilon_t$ & $\theta_t$ (no noise) \\ AR(p) & $\mathbb{R}^p$ (lags) & companion $G$ & $(1, 0, \dots, 0)\, \theta_t$ \\ HMM & $\{1, \dots, K\}$ & matrix $\mathbf{P}$ & $p(\cdot \mid \theta_{S_t}^*)$ \end{tabular}

nodes.title: AR(2) as SSM — worked example
nodes.content:
\textbf{\textcolor{red}{AR(2) AS A SSM --- WORKED EXAMPLE}}

How $G$ and $F$ actually work in the smallest non-trivial case where state augmentation does something.

\textbf{\textcolor{red}{Model.}}
\[ Y_t \;=\; \phi_1 Y_{t-1} + \phi_2 Y_{t-2} + \varepsilon_t. \]

\textbf{\textcolor{red}{State definition.}} Stack today's value with yesterday's value:
\[ \theta_t \;:=\; \begin{pmatrix} Y_t \\ Y_{t-1} \end{pmatrix} \in \mathbb{R}^2. \]
So at time $t-1$ the state is
\[ \theta_{t-1} \;=\; \begin{pmatrix} Y_{t-1} \\ Y_{t-2} \end{pmatrix}. \]

\textbf{\textcolor{red}{The matrices.}}
\[ G \;=\; \begin{pmatrix} \phi_1 & \phi_2 \\ 1 & 0 \end{pmatrix}, \qquad w_t \;=\; \begin{pmatrix} \varepsilon_t \\ 0 \end{pmatrix}, \qquad F \;=\; \begin{pmatrix} 1 & 0 \end{pmatrix}. \]

\textbf{\textcolor{red}{How $G$ works --- multiply it out.}}
\[ G\, \theta_{t-1} \;=\; \begin{pmatrix} \phi_1 & \phi_2 \\ 1 & 0 \end{pmatrix} \begin{pmatrix} Y_{t-1} \\ Y_{t-2} \end{pmatrix} \;=\; \begin{pmatrix} \phi_1 \cdot Y_{t-1} + \phi_2 \cdot Y_{t-2} \\ 1 \cdot Y_{t-1} + 0 \cdot Y_{t-2} \end{pmatrix} \;=\; \begin{pmatrix} \phi_1 Y_{t-1} + \phi_2 Y_{t-2} \\ Y_{t-1} \end{pmatrix}. \]
Now add $w_t$:
\[ \theta_t \;=\; G\, \theta_{t-1} + w_t \;=\; \begin{pmatrix} \phi_1 Y_{t-1} + \phi_2 Y_{t-2} + \varepsilon_t \\ Y_{t-1} + 0 \end{pmatrix} \;=\; \begin{pmatrix} Y_t \\ Y_{t-1} \end{pmatrix}.  \checkmark \]

\emph{Read the two rows separately:}

$\bullet$ \textbf{Row 1 of $G$}, $(\phi_1, \phi_2)$, combined with $\varepsilon_t$ in $w_t$, \emph{generates} today's $Y_t$ from yesterday's two values and a fresh shock. This row encodes the AR equation.

$\bullet$ \textbf{Row 2 of $G$}, $(1, 0)$, says: "the second component of $\theta_t$ equals the first component of $\theta_{t-1}$, with zero noise." So the previous top value $Y_{t-1}$ is just \emph{shifted down} into the bottom slot. That is the lag bookkeeping.

So $G$ does two jobs at once: \textbf{top row = AR dynamics}, \textbf{bottom rows = shift register that keeps the lags fresh}.

\textbf{\textcolor{red}{How $F$ works --- multiply it out.}}
\[ Y_t \;=\; F\, \theta_t \;=\; \begin{pmatrix} 1 & 0 \end{pmatrix} \begin{pmatrix} Y_t \\ Y_{t-1} \end{pmatrix} \;=\; 1 \cdot Y_t + 0 \cdot Y_{t-1} \;=\; Y_t.  \checkmark \]
The role of $F$ is to \emph{pick off} the component of $\theta_t$ that we actually observe --- the top one ($Y_t$). The bottom component ($Y_{t-1}$) sits inside the state but is \emph{not observed directly at time $t$}: it is there only because we need it to compute $Y_{t+1}$ in the next transition.

\textbf{\textcolor{red}{Why keep the second slot if $F$ throws it away?}}

The next transition needs it. Trace one step forward:
\[ \theta_{t+1} \;=\; G\, \theta_t + w_{t+1} \;=\; \begin{pmatrix} \phi_1 & \phi_2 \\ 1 & 0 \end{pmatrix} \begin{pmatrix} Y_t \\ Y_{t-1} \end{pmatrix} + \begin{pmatrix} \varepsilon_{t+1} \\ 0 \end{pmatrix} \;=\; \begin{pmatrix} \phi_1 Y_t + \phi_2 \cdot \mathbf{Y_{t-1}} + \varepsilon_{t+1} \\ Y_t \end{pmatrix}. \]
To generate $Y_{t+1}$ we need $Y_{t-1}$ (bold), which lives in the second slot of $\theta_t$. Dropping it after the emission at time $t$ would break the next AR step.

So the two slots play \emph{different roles}:

$\bullet$ \textbf{Top slot} = "the value emitted \emph{now}" --- read by $F$ at this time step.

$\bullet$ \textbf{Bottom slot} = "the value emitted \emph{last time}, kept around for \emph{next} time" --- read by row 1 of $G$ at the \emph{next} time step.

The bottom slot is a \emph{delay line / shift register}. Discarding it would throw away the memory the model needs to be Markov of order 1 in the state.

\textbf{\textcolor{red}{Mental picture.}}
\[ \theta_{t-1} = \begin{pmatrix} Y_{t-1} \\ Y_{t-2} \end{pmatrix} \;\xrightarrow{\;G,\, w_t\;}\; \theta_t = \begin{pmatrix} Y_t \\ Y_{t-1} \end{pmatrix} \;\xrightarrow{\;F\;}\; Y_t. \]

nodes.title: Bayesian statistics
nodes.content:
\textbf{\textcolor{red}{BAYESIAN STATISTICS --- Bayes' rule, derivation and intuition}}

You forecast the next value to be A. But you want to deal with uncertainty... the soltuon is probability

\textbf{\textcolor{red}{The goal.}} We want to know
\[ P(A \mid B), \]
i.e.\emph{"after seeing evidence $B$, how likely is hypothesis $A$?"}. 



\textbf{\textcolor{red}{From the definition of conditional probability.}} For two events $A, B$,
\[ P(A \mid B) \;=\; \frac{P(A \cap B)}{P(B)}, \qquad P(B \mid A) \;=\; \frac{P(A \cap B)}{P(A)}. \]
Read: "among the worlds where $B$ holds, what fraction also has $A$ ?"

\emph{The problem.} The joint $P(A \cap B)$ is usually hard to compute directly. Bayes' rule is the trick to express it in terms of quantities we can compute.

\textbf{\textcolor{red}{Derivation in three lines.}} Using:
\[ P(A \cap B) \;=\; P(A \mid B)\, P(B) \qquad \text{and} \qquad P(A \cap B) \;=\; P(B \mid A)\, P(A). \]
you get
\[ \boxed{\; P(A \mid B) \;=\; \frac{P(B \mid A)\, P(A)}{P(B)} \;} \qquad \text{(Bayes' rule)}. \]

\textbf{\textcolor{red}{Why Bayes' rule is brilliant.}} The genuine insight is the \emph{change of perspective}:
\[ \underbrace{P(A \cap B)}_{\text{hard to compute directly}} \;\;\longleftrightarrow\;\; \underbrace{P(B \mid A) \cdot P(A)}_{\text{both easy: a model + a prior}}. \]
The joint $P(A \cap B)$ --- "how often do hypothesis and evidence co-occur in the world" --- is rarely known in practice: it requires knowing the full bivariate distribution. But its two factorisations give us a way out:

$\bullet$ $P(A)$ is the \emph{prior}, something we can specify from background knowledge.

$\bullet$ $P(B \mid A)$ is the \emph{likelihood} --- "if hypothesis $A$ were true, how probable would the data $B$ be?" This is precisely what a \emph{model} (a hypothesis about how the data is generated) gives us for free. We don't observe whether $A$ is true, but we can simulate / compute the conditional distribution of $B$ under each candidate $A$.


\textbf{\textcolor{red}{Bayes' formula with names attached.}}
\[ \underbrace{P(A \mid B)}_{\text{posterior: belief in } A \text{ \emph{after} seeing } B} \;=\; \frac{\overbrace{P(B \mid A)}^{\text{likelihood: how compatible } B \text{ is with } A}\, \cdot \overbrace{P(A)}^{\text{prior: belief in } A \text{ \emph{before} seeing } B}}{\underbrace{P(B)}_{\text{evidence: marginal probability of } B}}. \]

Bayes is a form of learning from experience! 

\textbf{\textcolor{red}{Key reformulation --- the "evidence multiplier".}} Rewrite Bayes as
\[ P(A \mid B) \;=\; P(A) \;\cdot\; \underbrace{\frac{P(B \mid A)}{P(B)}}_{\text{evidence multiplier}}. \]

\emph{Reading.} The posterior equals the prior \emph{times} a ratio that compares "how likely was $B$ if $A$ were true" against "how likely was $B$ overall":

$\bullet$ \textbf{If $P(B \mid A) > P(B)$}: evidence is \emph{more} expected under $A$ than overall $\;\Rightarrow\;$ multiplier $>1$ $\;\Rightarrow\;$ \textbf{posterior $>$ prior}: belief in $A$ goes up.
...

So, new evicence comes in, there is a new testimony, and he says somethign that is more aligned with hyp A than overall distributin of possibel things he may have said. 

\emph{Why divide by $P(B)$?} Because some observations are common anyway: if $B$ happens regardless of $A$, seeing $B$ should not strongly convince us of $A$. The denominator corrects for the \emph{baseline frequency} of the evidence. Rare evidence is more informative than common evidence.


\textbf{\textcolor{red}{Probability vs likelihood --- one formula, two readings.}}

The expression $P(B \mid A)$ is \emph{literally} the same number whether you call it a probability or a likelihood. There is no different formula and no proportionality involved:
\[ L(A; B) \;=\; P(B \mid A). \]
The only thing that changes is what you keep fixed and what you treat as the argument:

$\bullet$ \emph{Probability reading.} $A$ is fixed, $B$ varies. Evaluating $P(B \mid A)$ tells you how likely each potential outcome $B$ is, under the assumed hypothesis $A$. Used for \emph{forward prediction}.

$\bullet$ \emph{Likelihood reading.} $B$ is fixed at the data we actually observed, $A$ varies. Now $P(B \mid A)$ is read as a function of $A$ --- it scores how well each candidate hypothesis explains the observed $B$. This is the reading in the Bayes context. 

\textbf{\textcolor{red}{Concrete example --- medical test.}}

$\bullet$ Disease prevalence: $P(D) = 0.01$.

$\bullet$ True positive rate: $P(+ \mid D) = 0.99$.

$\bullet$ False positive rate: $P(+ \mid \neg D) = 0.05$.

\emph{Question:} A patient tests positive. What is $P(D \mid +)$?

Bayes:
\[ P(D \mid +) \;=\; \frac{P(+ \mid D)\, P(D)}{P(+)}. \]
Denominator (law of total probability):
\[ P(+) \;=\; P(+ \mid D)\, P(D) + P(+ \mid \neg D)\, P(\neg D) \;=\; 0.99 \cdot 0.01 + 0.05 \cdot 0.99 \;=\; 0.0594. \]
So
\[ P(D \mid +) \;=\; \frac{0.99 \cdot 0.01}{0.0594} \;\approx\; 0.167. \]

\emph{Reading.} Even with a "99\% accurate" test, a positive result means only $\approx 17\%$ chance of having the disease --- because the disease is rare to start with. The prior $P(D) = 0.01$ is so small that the evidence multiplier $P(+ \mid D)/P(+) = 0.99 / 0.0594 \approx 16.7$ only pushes the posterior to $0.01 \times 16.7 \approx 0.17$.

\textbf{\textcolor{red}{Core Bayesian idea.}} Evidence must be interpreted \emph{relative to the baseline frequency}. Rare priors require strong evidence to overturn.

nodes.title: Bayesian vs frequentist inference
nodes.content:
\textbf{\textcolor{red}{BAYESIAN vs FREQUENTIST INFERENCE}}

After deriving Bayes' rule and seeing the prior get \emph{updated} by evidence into a posterior, a natural question arises: \emph{does the prior shift mean there is no true $\theta$?} The answer is no --- but to see why, we need to compare the two frameworks side by side.

\textbf{\textcolor{red}{The status of $\theta$.}}

$\bullet$ \emph{Frequentist.} $\theta$ is a \textbf{fixed unknown constant} of nature. It does not have a probability distribution. There is a true value, period. Probability is reserved for the data. Not a random variables.

$\bullet$ \emph{Bayesian.} $\theta$ may also be a fixed unknown constant in nature --- but since we don't \emph{know} it, we represent our \textbf{state of belief} about $\theta$ as a probability distribution: $\pi(\theta)$ before data, $p(\theta \mid y)$ after. The randomness lives in our \emph{knowledge} (is epistemic), not in $\theta$ itself. \theta is a random variable. 

So the prior shifting does \emph{not} mean $\theta$ moves. It means our \emph{uncertainty about $\theta$} sharpens around the values most compatible with the data. The true $\theta$ (if you believe in one) is a fixed point in parameter space; the probability mass representing our knowledge is what slides around it.

\textbf{\textcolor{red}{What is "random"? --- one-line slogan.}}
\[ \text{Frequentist: data is random, parameter is fixed.} \qquad \text{Bayesian: parameter and data are both modelled as random.} \]

\textbf{\textcolor{red}{Where uncertainty, that is, probability, is.}}

$\bullet$ \emph{Frequentist.} Ucertainty is driven by the samplig procedure (we see a different estimate just because the sample is not fully representative of the population)"$P(\hat\theta \in [a, b]) = 0.95$" means: if we repeated the sampling many times, 95\% of the resulting intervals $[\hat a_n, \hat b_n]$ would contain the true $\theta$.

$\bullet$ \emph{Bayesian.} Uncertainty is in (our knowledge of) the parameter itself updated by Bayes' rule. "$P(a < \theta < b \mid y) = 0.95$" means: \emph{given the data we observed}, our posterior distribution puts 95\% mass on $[a, b]$.

\textbf{\textcolor{red}{Confidence intervals (frequentist) vs Credible intervals (Bayesian).}}

\textbf{\textcolor{red}{Frequentist confidence interval --- exact formula.}} Given an estimator $\hat\theta_n$ with (asymptotic) standard error $\text{SE}(\hat\theta_n)$ (how the estimator estimates would vary across replicaitons of the experiment, derived analytically from the model), the $1 - \alpha$ Wald confidence interval is
\[ \text{CI}_{1-\alpha} \;=\; \bigl[\, \hat\theta_n - z_{\alpha/2} \cdot \text{SE}(\hat\theta_n),\;\; \hat\theta_n + z_{\alpha/2} \cdot \text{SE}(\hat\theta_n) \,\bigr], \]
where $z_{\alpha/2}$ is the $1 - \alpha/2$ quantile of the standard Normal (e.g.\ $z_{0.025} = 1.96$ for 95\%).

\emph{Where the $\sqrt{n}$ lives.} The standard error has the typical form $\text{SE}(\hat\theta_n) = \sigma / \sqrt{n}$ (with $\sigma$ the standard deviation of a single observation, or more generally $1/\sqrt{n\, I(\theta)}$ for the MLE). Substituting,
\[ \text{CI}_{1-\alpha} \;=\; \hat\theta_n \;\pm\; z_{\alpha/2} \cdot \frac{\sigma}{\sqrt{n}}. \]
So the interval shrinks at rate $1/\sqrt{n}$ as more data arrives --- more data $\Rightarrow$ tighter interval.



\textbf{\textcolor{red}{Bayesian credible interval --- exact formula.}} A $1 - \alpha$ credible interval is any interval $[a, b]$ such that the posterior probability
\[ P(\, a \le \theta \le b \mid y \,) \;=\; \int_{a}^{b} p(\theta \mid y)\, d\theta \;=\; 1 - \alpha. \]
Now $y$ is fixed (the observed data) and $\theta$ is the random variable; the probability is over the posterior $p(\theta \mid y)$.



\textbf{\textcolor{red}{Where does the prior come from? --- and does it bias things?}}

A common frequentist objection: "the prior is subjective, so the posterior is biased." Bayesian replies:

$\bullet$ The prior is a \emph{modelling choice}, like any other. Two analysts with different priors will reach different posteriors --- that is honest, not a bug.

$\bullet$ With enough data, the likelihood dominates and the posterior becomes essentially independent of the prior. In the limit, frequentist MLE and Bayesian posterior mode coincide.


\textbf{\textcolor{red}{Side-by-side summary.}}
\begin{tabular}{l|l|l} & Frequentist & Bayesian \\ \hline Status of $\theta$ & fixed unknown constant & random variable (uncertainty over) \\ Source of randomness & data only & data + parameter \\ Estimator of $\theta$ & MLE $\hat\theta$ & posterior $p(\theta \mid y)$ \\ Interval & confidence (over procedure) & credible (over $\theta$) \\ Updating with new data & re-run estimator & posterior $\to$ new prior, apply Bayes \end{tabular}

nodes.title: Lindley Paradox
nodes.content:
\textbf{\textcolor{red}{Lindley's paradox --- when the two frameworks loudly disagree.}}

A famous case where frequentist and Bayesian conclusions \emph{conflict} on the same data, especially when $n$ is large.

\textbf{Setup.} Test $H_0: \theta = \theta_0$ vs $H_1: \theta \ne \theta_0$, with sample mean $\hat\theta$ near (but not exactly equal to) $\theta_0$.

\textbf{Frequentist machinery.} The test statistic
\[ z = \frac{\hat\theta - \theta_0}{\sigma / \sqrt{n}} \]
contains $\sqrt{n}$. So for any fixed deviation $\hat\theta - \theta_0 \ne 0$, $z$ grows without bound as $n \to \infty$, and the p-value $\to 0$. With enough data, the test \emph{rejects} $H_0$ for any deviation, no matter how small.

\textbf{Bayesian machinery.} Under $H_1$, place a prior $\theta \sim \mathcal{N}(0, \tau^2)$. The Bayes factor is
\[ \text{BF}_{01} \;=\; \frac{p(y \mid H_0)}{p(y \mid H_1)}, \qquad p(y \mid H_1) \;=\; \int p(y \mid \theta)\, \pi(\theta \mid H_1)\, d\theta. \]
The integral averages over \emph{all} $\theta$ in the prior --- including the many values that do not fit $\hat\theta$. With a wide prior, only a tiny sliver near the data has high likelihood; the rest contributes almost nothing. So $H_1$ is \emph{penalised for being a vague hypothesis}: the marginal likelihood is dilute. In large samples this Occam penalty wins unless $H_1$ actually concentrates mass near the observed value.

\textbf{Concrete numbers.} $\sigma = 1$, $\theta_0 = 0$, $\hat\theta = 0.002$, $n = 1{,}000{,}000$, $\tau = 1$:
\[ z \;=\; 2 \;\Rightarrow\; p \;\approx\; 0.045  (\text{frequentist rejects at 5\%}), \]
\[ \text{BF}_{01} \;\approx\; \tau \sqrt{n} \cdot e^{-z^2/2} \;=\; 1000 \cdot e^{-2} \;\approx\; 135  (\text{Bayes factor: data 135}\times \text{ more likely under } H_0). \]

\emph{Same data, opposite conclusions:} frequentist rejects $H_0$, Bayesian strongly supports $H_0$.

\textbf{Why the disagreement?} The two methods answer \emph{different questions}.

$\bullet$ \emph{Frequentist}: "How extreme is the data assuming $H_0$?" With huge $n$, even practically negligible deviations look extreme.

$\bullet$ \emph{Bayesian}: "Which hypothesis predicts the data better, on average?" The vague $H_1$ pays an Occam penalty for spreading prior mass over values that no longer fit.

\textbf{Intuition in one line.}
\[ \text{Frequentist asks: \emph{is the true } \theta \text{ exactly } \theta_0?} \Longleftrightarrow \text{Bayesian asks: \emph{is the data well explained by } \theta_0 \text{ vs by an averaged-over } H_1?} \]

\textbf{Practical message.}

$\bullet$ For \emph{small to moderate $n$} the two frameworks usually agree numerically.

$\bullet$ For \emph{very large $n$} (high-frequency finance, genomics, particle physics), p-values reject everything --- Bayes factors are preferred for model selection.

$\bullet$ This is not a numerical fluke: it is a real difference in what "evidence" means in each framework. Use the framework whose question matches what you actually want to know.

nodes.content:
\textbf{\textcolor{red}{PREDICTION --- how Bayesian concepts give us all the formulas}}

THIS IS YOUR FINAL AIM 

Recalling that a bayesian forecat is: 
\[ P(\, a \le \theta \le b \mid y \,) \;=\; \int_{a}^{b} f(\theta \mid y)\, d\theta \;=\; 1 - \alpha. \]
Now $y$ is fixed (the observed data) and $\theta$ is the random variable; the probability is over the posterior $f(\theta \mid y)$.

\emph{Where does the predictive density come from?} By the definition of a conditional density (chain rule applied to the joint of $n+1$ observations):
\[ f(y_{n+1} \mid y_{1:n}) \;=\; \frac{f(y_{1:n+1})}{f(y_{1:n})}. \]
This is the natural starting point, but \emph{both} densities on the right are usually intractable directly --- each requires integrating the full joint over all latent quantities. The trick is to introduce $\theta$ (parameter or state) into the picture and marginalise it out instead, which gives the closed posterior-predictive form below. 

\emph{General version (textbook posterior predictive).} For observed data $y_{1:n}$, future observation $y_{n+1}$, and latent quantity $\theta$ (parameter or state):
\[ \boxed{\; f(y_{n+1} \mid y_{1:n}) \;=\; \int f(y_{n+1},\, \theta \mid y_{1:n})\, d\theta \;=\; \int f(y_{n+1} \mid y_{1:n}, \theta)\, f(\theta \mid y_{1:n})\, d\theta. \;} \]

\emph{Why we can "introduce" $\theta$.} The first equality is just the marginalisation identity $f(A) = \int f(A, B)\, dB$, which holds for \emph{any} $B$ --- independent or not. Mathematically the introduction is always legal. Practically it is useful precisely because $y_{n+1}$ \emph{depends on} $\theta$ via the model, so the resulting joint factors into computable pieces (likelihood $\times$ posterior).
 

\emph{SSM specialisation.} In a state-space model the latent is the contemporaneous state $\theta := \theta_{n+1}$, and the emission's conditional independence $f(y_{n+1} \mid \theta_{n+1}, y_{1:n}) = f(y_{n+1} \mid \theta_{n+1})$ lets us drop $y_{1:n}$ from the conditional, giving \emph{Integral form of the predictive distribution} (posterior predictive):
\[ \boxed{\; f(y_{n+1} \mid y_{1:n}) \;=\; \int f(y_{n+1} \mid \theta_{n+1})\, \underbrace{f(\theta_{n+1} \mid y_{1:n})}_{\text{need to retrive this with filtering and}}, d\theta_{n+1}. \;} \]
Note the integration variabel must watch what's varying in the integrand. 

\emph{Reading.} KEY:  For each candidate value of the contemporaneous state $\theta_{n+1}$, the emission gives a forecast $f(y_{n+1} \mid \theta_{n+1})$; we average these forecasts, weighted by how plausible each $\theta_{n+1}$ is given the data we have already seen ($f(\theta_{n+1} \mid y_{1:n})$, the predicted-state distribution).

\emph{Closed form in the Gaussian case.} If the posterior of the latent is Gaussian
\[ \theta \mid y_{1:n} \;\sim\; \mathcal{N}(m_n,\, C_n), \qquad m_n \;=\; E[\theta \mid y_{1:n}], \]
and the emission is Gaussian with observation noise $\varepsilon_{n+1} \sim \mathcal{N}(0, \sigma^2)$ independent of $\theta$ (so $Y_{n+1} = \theta + \varepsilon_{n+1}$ given $\theta$), then the predictive distribution evaluates in closed form to
\[ \boxed{\; Y_{n+1} \mid y_{1:n} \;\sim\; \mathcal{N}\bigl(m_n,\; C_n + \sigma^2\bigr). \;} \]

\emph{Why?} Two reasons combine.

$\bullet$ \emph{Sum of independent Gaussians is Gaussian.} Decompose $Y_{n+1} = \theta + \varepsilon_{n+1}$. Conditional on $y_{1:n}$, $\theta$ is Gaussian (posterior $\mathcal{N}(m_n, C_n)$) and $\varepsilon_{n+1}$ is Gaussian and independent of $\theta$. Their sum is therefore Gaussian.

$\bullet$ \emph{Means and variances add.}
\[ E[Y_{n+1} \mid y_{1:n}] \;=\; E[\theta \mid y_{1:n}] + E[\varepsilon_{n+1}] \;=\; m_n + 0 \;=\; m_n. \]
\[ \text{Var}(Y_{n+1} \mid y_{1:n}) \;=\; \underbrace{\text{Var}(\theta \mid y_{1:n})}_{C_n} \;+\; \underbrace{\text{Var}(\varepsilon_{n+1})}_{\sigma^2} \;=\; C_n + \sigma^2. \]


\emph{Variance has two terms, with meanings.}

$\bullet$ $C_n$ --- \emph{parameter / state uncertainty}: we don't know $\theta$ exactly, only the posterior $\mathcal{N}(m_n, C_n)$.

$\bullet$ $\sigma^2$ --- \emph{future observation noise}: even if we knew $\theta$ exactly, $Y_{n+1}$ would still have noise.

Adding them is the Bayesian honesty about uncertainty: forecast bands include both. The frequentist plug-in $Y_{n+1} \mid \hat\theta \sim \mathcal{N}(\hat\theta, \sigma^2)$ keeps only the $\sigma^2$ term and produces bands that are too narrow. IT IS SO OBVIOUS THE FREQUENTIST IS WRONG, JUT BECAUSE BEING $\hat \theta$ ESTIMATED it cannot be used as a fixed point. Note frequentists fixed this by a correction for estiamtion uncertainty. 



-------------------

TO REACH PREDICITON , WE NEED TO DERIVE THE COMPONENT $f(\theta_{n+1} \mid y_{1:n})$

NOW WE USE BAYES RULE: 


\textbf{\textcolor{red}{1. Filtering (state estimation)} $\;\;f(\theta_t \mid y_{1:t})$.} \emph{What is the state today, given everything observed up to today?} Incremental Bayes applied to the new observation $y_t$:
\[ f(\theta_t \mid y_{1:t}) \;\propto\; \underbrace{f(y_t \mid \theta_t)}_{\text{likelihood of \emph{new} datum only}} \;\cdot\; \underbrace{f(\theta_t \mid y_{1:t-1})}_{\text{prior carried forward}}. \]
\emph{Why only $y_t$ in the likelihood?} Past data $y_{1:t-1}$ are \emph{already in the prior} $f(\theta_t \mid y_{1:t-1})$ --- including them in the likelihood would double-count. Future data $y_{t+1:T}$ don't exist yet (filtering is online). So at each step the new likelihood is just the emission of the single new datum.

The "prior carried forward" is yesterday's filtered posterior pushed through the transition kernel:
\[ f(\theta_t \mid y_{1:t-1}) \;=\; \int f(\theta_t \mid \theta_{t-1})\, f(\theta_{t-1} \mid y_{1:t-1})\, d\theta_{t-1}. \]
\emph{Step pattern} (the entire filter): \textbf{predict} (transition forward) $\to$ \textbf{update} (Bayes with new $y_t$). Repeat forever.

\emph{Equivalent batch form (textbook / iid case).} When $\theta$ is a static parameter and observations are conditionally iid given $\theta$, you can write the posterior in one shot using all data and the original prior:
\[ f(\theta \mid y_{1:n}) \;\propto\; f(y_{1:n} \mid \theta) \cdot f(\theta) \;\underbrace{=}_{\text{iid}}\; \prod_{t=1}^{n} f(y_t \mid \theta) \cdot f(\theta). \]
\emph{Same answer, different bookkeeping:} the incremental form uses \emph{yesterday's posterior $\times$ new datum's likelihood} at each step; the batch form uses \emph{the original prior $\times$ the product of all likelihoods} once. The two agree by telescoping --- "multiplying likelihoods one-by-one = multiplying them all at once."

\emph{Where iid matters.} The batch product-of-likelihoods step needs iid. In an \emph{SSM} the observations are \emph{not} iid (they share a time-varying state), so the batch form has to be written conditional on the entire latent path: $f(y_{1:T} \mid \theta_{0:T}) = \prod_t f(y_t \mid \theta_t)$. Same product structure, but now indexed by the time-varying state, which is exactly what the filtering recursion exploits step by step.


\textbf{\textcolor{red}{2. State prediction} $\;\;f(\theta_{t+h} \mid y_{1:t})$.} \emph{Where will the hidden state be $h$ steps from now?} Just keep applying the transition kernel, no new evidence:
\[ f(\theta_{t+1} \mid y_{1:t}) \;=\; \int f(\theta_{t+1} \mid \theta_t)\, f(\theta_t \mid y_{1:t})\, d\theta_t, \]
and recursively
\[ f(\theta_{t+h} \mid y_{1:t}) \;=\; \int f(\theta_{t+h} \mid \theta_{t+h-1})\, f(\theta_{t+h-1} \mid y_{1:t})\, d\theta_{t+h-1}. \]
\emph{Reading.} This is just the "predict" half of the filter, run $h$ times without any "update" step. Uncertainty grows as $h$ grows.

\textbf{\textcolor{red}{3. Observation prediction} $\;\;f(y_{t+h} \mid y_{1:t})$.} \emph{What value will we observe $h$ steps from now?} Marginalise the future state out of the joint $(y_{t+h}, \theta_{t+h})$:
\[ f(y_{t+h} \mid y_{1:t}) \;=\; \int f(y_{t+h} \mid \theta_{t+h})\, f(\theta_{t+h} \mid y_{1:t})\, d\theta_{t+h}. \]
\emph{Reading.} Plug each candidate state $\theta_{t+h}$ into the emission to get a forecast distribution conditional on that state; weight by how likely that state is given the data so far; integrate. This is the \textbf{posterior predictive} from the Bayesian-statistics snippet, applied to the SSM.

\textbf{\textcolor{red}{4. Smoothing} $\;\;f(\theta_t \mid y_{1:T})$.} \emph{Looking back, what was the state at time $t$ given all data including the future?} Bayes again, this time using future data to refine our belief about $\theta_t$:
\[ f(\theta_t \mid y_{1:T}) \;=\; f(\theta_t \mid y_{1:t}) \;\cdot\; \frac{f(y_{t+1:T} \mid \theta_t)}{f(y_{t+1:T} \mid y_{1:t})}, \]
i.e.\ multiply the filtered posterior by the likelihood of the future (given $\theta_t$), then renormalise. The forward--backward algorithm computes this efficiently by running a forward filter then a backward pass.

\textbf{\textcolor{red}{5. Decoding (HMM only)} $\;\;\arg\max_{s_{0:T}} f(s_{0:T} \mid y_{1:T})$.} \emph{Most likely path of hidden states.} By Bayes, $f(s_{0:T} \mid y_{1:T}) \propto f(y_{1:T} \mid s_{0:T})\, f(s_{0:T})$, and we already computed both factors when deriving the likelihood (equation $(2)$ in the Estimation snippet). Maximisation over $s_{0:T}$ is done by dynamic programming (Viterbi). For DLMs the joint is Gaussian and the joint mode equals the vector of marginal means --- so smoothing already gives the decoded path.

\textbf{\textcolor{red}{6. Likelihood (for parameter estimation)} $\;\;f(y_{1:T} \mid \phi)$.} \emph{If the model has unknown parameters $\phi$.} Marginalise out the hidden path:
\[ f(y_{1:T} \mid \phi) \;=\; \int f(y_{1:T},\, \theta_{0:T} \mid \phi)\, d\theta_{0:T}. \]
This is the building block for both:

$\bullet$ \emph{Frequentist}: maximise over $\phi$ to get the MLE $\hat\phi$.

$\bullet$ \emph{Bayesian}: combine with a prior $\pi(\phi)$ via Bayes' rule, $f(\phi \mid y_{1:T}) \propto f(y_{1:T} \mid \phi)\, \pi(\phi)$.

\textbf{\textcolor{red}{Putting parameter uncertainty into prediction.}}

$\bullet$ \emph{Frequentist plug-in.} Take $\hat\phi$, then compute $f(y_{n+1} \mid y_{1:n}, \hat\phi)$ by the rules above. \emph{Pretends $\hat\phi$ is the truth} --- forecast bands too narrow.

$\bullet$ \emph{Bayesian posterior predictive.} Integrate out $\phi$:
\[ f(y_{n+1} \mid y_{1:n}) \;=\; \int f(y_{n+1} \mid y_{1:n}, \phi)\, f(\phi \mid y_{1:n})\, d\phi. \]
This is just \emph{Bayes' rule applied twice}: once to get the filtered/predicted state distribution given $\phi$, then again to integrate out the parameter. Forecast bands honestly account for parameter uncertainty.

\textbf{\textcolor{red}{Master pattern.}} Every prediction formula in this chapter is one of two operations on the SSM joint:

$\bullet$ \textbf{Condition} on something we observed (likelihood) and \textbf{multiply} by what we believed before (prior) --- that is Bayes' rule, gives the posterior.

$\bullet$ \textbf{Marginalise} (integrate / sum) over what we don't care about --- gives the relevant marginal or predictive distribution.

\textbf{\textcolor{red}{Worked example (HMM weather/activity).}} The recursion we used in the filtering exercise,
\[ \alpha_t(j) \;=\; \underbrace{b_{j, y_t}}_{\text{likelihood of new obs}} \;\cdot\; \underbrace{\sum_{i} \alpha_{t-1}(i)\, p_{i,j}}_{\text{prior carried forward}}, \]
is exactly the SSM filtering formula above, with discrete states. The \emph{predict} half (the sum) propagates yesterday's belief through $\mathbf{P}$; the \emph{update} half (the multiplication by $b_{j, y_t}$) is Bayes applied to today's observation.

\textbf{\textcolor{red}{Bottom line.}} There is only one engine: \emph{posterior $\propto$ likelihood $\cdot$ prior}, with marginalisation to remove unwanted variables. Filtering, smoothing, prediction, decoding, MLE, posterior predictive --- each is just that engine pointed at a different conditional or marginal of the SSM joint.

nodes.content:
\textbf{\textcolor{red}{WORKED EXAMPLE --- RW + noise with fixed hidden state (N

\textbf{\textcolor{red}{Three readings of the Kalman gain $K_n$.}}

$\bullet$ \textbf{(1) Fraction of the prediction error you use.} $m_n = m_{n-1} + K_n\,e_n$. $K_n \in (0,1)$ tells you what fraction of the surprise $e_n$ gets folded into the estimate: $K_n = 1$ snaps to $y_n$, $K_n = 0$ keeps $m_{n-1}$, $K_n = 0.3$ moves $30\%$ of the way.

$\bullet$ \textbf{(2) Ratio of variances (signal-to-total).}
\[ K_n \;=\; \frac{C_{n-1}}{C_{n-1} + \sigma^2} \;=\; \frac{\text{prior variance of state}}{\text{predictive variance of obs}}. \]
Of the total variability of $Y_n$, what fraction comes from \emph{state uncertainty} (informative about $\theta_n$) vs \emph{observation noise} (uninformative)? State dominates $\Rightarrow K_n \to 1$; noise dominates $\Rightarrow K_n \to 0$.

$\bullet$ \textbf{(3) Share of posterior precision contributed by the new datum.}
\[ K_n \;=\; \frac{1/\sigma^2}{1/C_{n-1} + 1/\sigma^2} \;=\; \frac{\text{data precision}}{\text{posterior precision}}. \]
$K_n$ is the fraction of total information that the new observation supplies. Sharp data $\Rightarrow$ big share $\Rightarrow$ big update; noisy data $\Rightarrow$ small share $\Rightarrow$ small update.

\emph{One-liner:} $ K_n \;=\; \dfrac{\text{how much the data tells you}}{\text{everything you know after seeing it}}$ --- the weight of the new evidence in the final answer.
ormal--Normal conjugate)}}

\textbf{\textcolor{red}{Setup --- full RW + noise, then specialise to fixed state.}} Start from the full local-level state-space model.

$\bullet$ \emph{State equation (random walk):} $\theta_t \;=\; \theta_{t-1} + w_t, \qquad w_t \overset{\text{iid}}{\sim} \mathcal{N}(0,\, W),$ with $\theta_0 \sim \mathcal{N}(m_0, C_0)$.

$\bullet$ \emph{Observation equation:} $Y_t \;=\; \theta_t + \varepsilon_t, \qquad \varepsilon_t \overset{\text{iid}}{\sim} \mathcal{N}(0, \sigma^2).$

All errors $\{w_t\}, \{\varepsilon_t\}$ and the initial state $\theta_0$ are \emph{mutually independent}.

\emph{Simplification --- fix the state.} Set the state-noise variance to zero, $W = 0$. Then $w_t = 0$ almost surely, so $\theta_t = \theta_{t-1} = \dots = \theta_0$ for every $t$. The state collapses to the single unknown value $\theta \equiv \theta_0$, and the model reduces to
\[ \theta \sim \mathcal{N}(m_0, C_0), \qquad Y_t \;=\; \theta + \varepsilon_t, \qquad \varepsilon_t \overset{\text{iid}}{\sim} \mathcal{N}(0, \sigma^2). \]
This is the constant-mean Gaussian model with a Gaussian conjugate prior --- the simplest non-trivial Bayesian setting.

\textbf{Distributional reading.} Conditional on $\theta$, the observations are iid Gaussian: $Y_1, Y_2, \dots, Y_n \mid \theta \overset{\text{iid}}{\sim} \mathcal{N}(\theta, \sigma^2)$.

\textbf{\textcolor{red}{Goal.}} Compute the posterior $f(\theta \mid y_{1:n})$.

\textbf{\textcolor{red}{Derivation (batch form).}} Apply Bayes' rule, then use iid to factor the likelihood as a product:
\[ f(\theta \mid y_{1:n}) \;\propto\; f(y_{1:n} \mid \theta) \cdot \pi(\theta) \;=\; \prod_{t=1}^{n} f(y_t \mid \theta) \cdot \pi(\theta). \]

\emph{Step 1 --- plug in the Gaussian densities.}
\[ f(\theta \mid y_{1:n}) \;\propto\; \exp\!\Big(-\frac{1}{2\sigma^2}\sum_{t=1}^n (y_t - \theta)^2\Big) \;\cdot\; \exp\!\Big(-\frac{(\theta - m_0)^2}{2 C_0}\Big). \]

\emph{Step 2 --- expand $\sum (y_t - \theta)^2$.} Using $\bar y = \tfrac{1}{n}\sum_t y_t$,
\[ \sum_{t=1}^n (y_t - \theta)^2 \;=\; n\theta^2 - 2 n \bar y\, \theta + \sum_{t=1}^n y_t^2. \]
The $\sum y_t^2$ does not depend on $\theta$ --- it is absorbed into the normalising constant.

\emph{Step 3 --- collect $\theta^2$ and $\theta$ terms.}
\[ \log f(\theta \mid y_{1:n}) \;\stackrel{\theta}{=}\; -\frac{1}{2}\Bigl[\, \theta^2 \Bigl(\tfrac{1}{C_0} + \tfrac{n}{\sigma^2}\Bigr) \;-\; 2\theta \Bigl(\tfrac{m_0}{C_0} + \tfrac{n \bar y}{\sigma^2}\Bigr) \,\Bigr] + \text{const}. \]

\emph{Step 4 --- match the generic Gaussian kernel} $\log \mathcal{N}(\theta; m, C) \stackrel{\theta}{=} -\tfrac{1}{2}\bigl[\theta^2 \cdot \tfrac{1}{C} - 2\theta \cdot \tfrac{m}{C}\bigr] + \text{const}$. Reading off coefficients:
\[ \boxed{\; \frac{1}{C_n} \;=\; \frac{1}{C_0} + \frac{n}{\sigma^2}, \qquad \frac{m_n}{C_n} \;=\; \frac{m_0}{C_0} + \frac{n \bar y}{\sigma^2} \;\Longrightarrow\; m_n \;=\; C_n\Bigl(\tfrac{m_0}{C_0} + \tfrac{n \bar y}{\sigma^2}\Bigr). \;} \]
Hence
\[ \boxed{\; \theta \mid y_{1:n} \;\sim\; \mathcal{N}\bigl(m_n,\, C_n\bigr), \qquad m_n = E[\theta \mid y_{1:n}], \qquad C_n = \mathrm{Var}(\theta \mid y_{1:n}). \;} \]

\textbf{\textcolor{red}{Fully-expanded forms.}} Inverting the precision and plugging in,
\[ \boxed{\; C_n \;=\; \frac{1}{\tfrac{1}{C_0} + \tfrac{n}{\sigma^2}} \;=\; \frac{C_0 \, \sigma^2}{\sigma^2 + n\, C_0}, \qquad m_n \;=\; \frac{\sigma^2\, m_0 \;+\; n\, C_0\, \bar y}{\sigma^2 + n\, C_0}. \;} \]


\textbf{\textcolor{red}{Posterior precision $1/C_n$.}} The precision \emph{adds}:
\[ \underbrace{\frac{1}{C_n}}_{\text{posterior precision}} \;=\; \underbrace{\frac{1}{C_0}}_{\text{prior precision}} \;+\; \underbrace{\frac{n}{\sigma^2}}_{\text{data precision}}. \]
Because both terms are non-negative, $1/C_n \ge 1/C_0$ always --- the posterior is \emph{always} at least as precise as the prior. Even poor-quality data (large $\sigma^2$) adds some information, just less of it. Sharper data ($\sigma^2$ small) or more data ($n$ large) makes the posterior sharper. The lower the variance of Cn th ebetter!  ()

\textbf{\textcolor{red}{Posterior mean $m_n$ as a weighted average.}} Rewrite $m_n$:
\[ m_n \;=\; \underbrace{\frac{1/C_0}{1/C_0 + n/\sigma^2}}_{\text{prior weight}} \cdot m_0 \;+\; \underbrace{\frac{n/\sigma^2}{1/C_0 + n/\sigma^2}}_{\text{data weight}} \cdot \bar y. \]
$m_n$ is a convex combination of the \emph{prior mean} $m_0 = E[\theta]$ and the \emph{sample mean} $\bar y$, with weights proportional to the respective precisions (frequentist would just have used the sample mean).

\textbf{\textcolor{red}{Recursive (one-step-at-a-time) derivation.}} Index the latent state by time, $\theta_n$, even though in this fixed-state model $\theta_n = \theta_{n-1} = \dots = \theta_0$ a.s. The same posterior can be obtained incrementally by applying the filtering recursion
\[ f(\theta_n \mid y_{1:n}) \;\propto\; \underbrace{f(y_n \mid \theta_n)}_{\text{new datum's likelihood}} \;\cdot\; \underbrace{f(\theta_n \mid y_{1:n-1})}_{\text{prior carried forward}}. \]
In the fixed-state case the transition is the identity ($W=0$), so the carried-forward prior is simply the previous step's posterior:
\[ \theta_n \mid y_{1:n-1} \;\sim\; \mathcal{N}(m_{n-1}, C_{n-1}) \qquad (\text{with } m_0, C_0 \text{ at } n=1). \]

\emph{Update with $y_n$.} Apply Bayes with the carried-forward prior as prior and the new datum as likelihood.

\emph{Step 1 --- Bayes:} $f(\theta_n \mid y_{1:n}) \propto f(y_n \mid \theta_n)\, f(\theta_n \mid y_{1:n-1})$. The likelihood $f(y_n \mid \theta_n)$ comes directly from the observation equation $Y_n = \theta_n + \varepsilon_n$ with $\varepsilon_n \sim \mathcal{N}(0, \sigma^2)$: conditional on $\theta_n$, $Y_n \sim \mathcal{N}(\theta_n, \sigma^2)$.

\emph{Reminder --- Gaussian density.} A $\mathcal{N}(\mu, v)$ density evaluated at $x$ is
\[ \mathcal{N}(x; \mu, v) \;=\; \tfrac{1}{\sqrt{2\pi v}} \exp\!\Bigl(-\tfrac{(x - \mu)^2}{2 v}\Bigr). \]

\emph{Step 2 --- plug in Gaussians:}
\[ f(\theta_n \mid y_{1:n}) \;\propto\; \exp\!\Bigl(-\tfrac{(y_n - \theta_n)^2}{2\sigma^2}\Bigr) \cdot \exp\!\Bigl(-\tfrac{(\theta_n - m_{n-1})^2}{2 C_{n-1}}\Bigr). \]

\emph{Step 3 --- collect $\theta_n^2, \theta_n$ terms:}
\[ \log f(\theta_n \mid y_{1:n}) \;\stackrel{\theta_n}{=}\; -\tfrac{1}{2}\Bigl[\,\theta_n^2\bigl(\tfrac{1}{C_{n-1}} + \tfrac{1}{\sigma^2}\bigr) - 2\theta_n\bigl(\tfrac{m_{n-1}}{C_{n-1}} + \tfrac{y_n}{\sigma^2}\bigr)\,\Bigr] + \text{const}. \]

\emph{Step 4 --- match $-\tfrac{1}{2}\bigl[\theta_n^2/C - 2\theta_n m/C\bigr]$ and read off coefficients:}
\[ \boxed{\; \frac{1}{C_n} \;=\; \frac{1}{C_{n-1}} + \frac{1}{\sigma^2}, \qquad m_n \;=\; C_n\Bigl(\tfrac{m_{n-1}}{C_{n-1}} + \tfrac{y_n}{\sigma^2}\Bigr), \qquad \theta_n \mid y_{1:n} \;\sim\; \mathcal{N}(m_n, C_n). \;} \]

\emph{Forecast $Y_{n+1}$ (after filtering).} With the just-obtained posterior $\theta_n \mid y_{1:n} \sim \mathcal{N}(m_n, C_n)$ and $Y_{n+1} = \theta_{n+1} + \varepsilon_{n+1} = \theta_n + \varepsilon_{n+1}$ (fixed state), sum of independent Gaussians gives
\[ \boxed{\; Y_{n+1} \mid y_{1:n} \;\sim\; \mathcal{N}(m_n,\; C_n + \sigma^2). \;} \]
This is the standard one-step-ahead predictive of the next observation, with mean $f_{n+1} = m_n$ and variance $Q_{n+1} = C_n + \sigma^2$.

\textbf{\textcolor{red}{Prediction-error correction (Kalman) form.}} Algebraically simplifying the precision-blend formula for $m_n$ gives the interpretable Kalman update
\[ \boxed{\; m_n \;=\; m_{n-1} + K_n\, \underbrace{(y_n - m_{n-1})}_{e_n \,=\, \text{prediction error}}, \qquad K_n \;=\; \frac{C_{n-1}}{C_{n-1} + \sigma^2}. \;} \]
Here $e_n = y_n - m_{n-1}$ is the innovation. Note how Kn goes  up (we trust the new observation) if reliability is high.

\textbf{\textcolor{red}{Two readings of the Kalman gain $K_n$.}}

$\bullet$ \textbf{(1) Ratio of variances (signal-to-total).}

Of the total variability of $Y_n$, what fraction comes from \emph{state uncertainty} (informative about $\theta_n$) vs \emph{observation noise} (uninformative)? State dominates $\Rightarrow K_n \to 1$; noise dominates $\Rightarrow K_n \to 0$.

nodes.title: Parameter Estimation
SSM flexibility — no stationarity required
nodes.content:
\textbf{\textcolor{red}{SSM FLEXIBILITY --- why no stationarity requirement}}

\textbf{\textcolor{red}{Why ARMA cannot fit a non-stationary series.}} ARMA models a process with \emph{constant} parameters $(\phi_i, \theta_j, \sigma^2)$. A model with constant parameters can only describe data whose statistical properties are themselves constant in time: constant mean, constant variance, autocovariance depending only on the lag. That is exactly the definition of weak stationarity.

If the data has a trend (mean drifting upward), seasonality (mean cycling), or changing volatility (variance growing), there is \emph{no choice} of constants $(\phi_i, \theta_j, \sigma^2)$ that can reproduce it --- because constants cannot represent a moving target. 

\emph{Practical recipe with ARMA:} first remove the non-stationary features (differencing $\to$ ARIMA, deseasonalising $\to$ SARIMA, detrending) so that the residual series is stationary; only then fit ARMA.



\textbf{\textcolor{red}{Why SSMs do not.}} An SSM separates two concerns:
\[ \theta_t = G_t \theta_{t-1} + w_t  (\text{state evolves}), \qquad Y_t = F_t \theta_t + v_t  (\text{observation snapshot}). \]
The state $\theta_t$ itself is allowed to be \emph{non-stationary}; the observation inherits that non-stationarity. Non-stationary behaviour is encoded directly inside $\theta_t$.

\textbf{\textcolor{red}{Flexibility: stack components in the state vector.}} The state can be assembled from independent blocks, each contributing its own structure:

$\bullet$ \emph{Trend block:} $\mu_t = \mu_{t-1} + \beta_{t-1} + w_{1,t}$, $\beta_t = \beta_{t-1} + w_{2,t}$ --- a level $\mu_t$ that drifts with a slope $\beta_t$ that itself drifts.

$\bullet$ \emph{Seasonal block:} $s_t + s_{t-1} + \dots + s_{t-S+2} = w_t$ (dummy form), or trigonometric Fourier components --- periodicity built in.

$\bullet$ \emph{Regression block:} $\alpha_t = \alpha_{t-1} + w_t$ multiplied by a covariate $x_t$ in $F_t$ --- regression coefficient evolving in time.

$\bullet$ \emph{AR / autoregressive block:} state contains lagged values, transition is the companion matrix.

Stacked: $\theta_t = (\mu_t,\, \beta_t,\, s_t,\, s_{t-1},\, \dots,\, \alpha_t,\, \dots)^\top$, and $Y_t = F_t \theta_t + v_t$ picks the relevant linear combination. Each block evolves independently, and $Y_t$ is their joint output plus noise.

\textbf{\textcolor{red}{The cleanest contrast.}}

\begin{tabular}{l|l|l} & ARMA & SSM \\ \hline Models & correlation structure of $Y_t$ directly & generative mechanism producing $Y_t$ \\ Parameters & constant in $t$ & can be time-varying \\ State / memory & implicit in lagged $Y$'s & explicit in $\theta_t$ \\ Trend, seasonality & must be removed first & encoded in $\theta_t$ \\ Non-stationary data & not supported & natively supported \end{tabular}

\textbf{\textcolor{red}{Intuition --- model the system, not the symptoms.}} ARMA describes how $Y_t$ correlates with its own past, summarised by a few constants; that only works if those correlations don't drift. SSMs describe \emph{what is producing} $Y_t$ --- a latent dynamical system whose own evolution can have trend, drift, seasonal swings, regime switches. Whatever pattern of correlations comes out is a \emph{consequence} of the chosen state dynamics, not a constraint on the model class.

\emph{Exam relevance.} The May 2021 CO\textsubscript{2} question asks exactly this: trend + seasonality in the raw data, can you use a DLM \emph{without} preliminary transformation? Answer: \textbf{yes}, because trend and seasonal components live inside the state and are estimated jointly with everything else --- no detrending, no deseasonalising required.


\textbf{\textcolor{red}{Aside --- if you let ARMA's parameters drift, you get an SSM.}} The cleanest way to see SSM as the strict superset of ARMA is to let the ARMA coefficients become time-varying.

$\bullet$ \textbf{Step 1 --- make ARMA time-varying.} Replace constants with functions of $t$:
\[ Y_t \;=\; \phi_1(t)\, Y_{t-1} + \dots + \phi_p(t)\, Y_{t-p} + \varepsilon_t + \theta_1(t)\, \varepsilon_{t-1} + \dots, \qquad \varepsilon_t \sim \mathcal{N}(0, \sigma_t^2). \]
On its own this is ill-posed: infinitely many parameters, unidentifiable from finite data.

$\bullet$ \textbf{Step 2 --- give the coefficients their own evolution.} Treat $\phi_i(t), \theta_j(t), \sigma_t^2$ as random processes --- typically random walks:
\[ \phi_i(t) \;=\; \phi_i(t-1) + \eta_{i,t}, \qquad \eta_{i,t} \sim \mathcal{N}(0, q_i). \]

$\bullet$ \textbf{Step 3 --- stack into a state vector.} Let
\[ \theta_t \;=\; \bigl(\underbrace{Y_t, Y_{t-1}, \dots, Y_{t-p+1}}_{\text{lagged values}},\; \underbrace{\phi_1(t), \dots, \phi_p(t)}_{\text{time-varying coeffs}},\; \dots\bigr)^\top. \]
Both the lagged data and the coefficients now live inside the state. The state equation handles their joint evolution; the observation equation $Y_t = F_t \theta_t + v_t$ picks the right linear combination. This is a DLM (linear Gaussian SSM); the products $Y_{t-1}\, \phi_1(t)$ are handled either by treating $Y_{t-1}$ as a known regressor (giving a \emph{dynamic regression / TVP-regression DLM}) or via a nonlinear SSM (extended/unscented Kalman, particle filter).

trash.title: Detrending
trash.content:
\textbf{\textcolor{red}{DETRENDING}}

Having fitted $\widehat{T}_t$, write
\[ y_t = \widehat{T}_t + E_t, \quad t = 2, \dots, n. \]
Remove the trend to obtain the de-trended series:
\[ y_t^{\text{detrended}} = y_t - \widehat{T}_t. \]

trash.title: SES: no uncertainty, multi-dim P_t
Special cases of α (SES)
trash.content:
If $\alpha = 1$: $\hat{y}_{t+1\mid t} = y_t$ \quad (naive forecast = last obs).

If $\alpha = 0$: $\hat{y}_{t+1\mid t} = \hat{y}_{t\mid t-1}$ \quad (constant forecast, ignore new data).

In practice tune $\alpha$ on a training sample, e.g.\ minimize MSE.

trash.title: Tuning α via predictive performance
Statistical model = joint law
trash.content:
$\to$ Defining a \textbf{statistical model} for a stoch.\ process means specifying the joint probability law of $(Y_t)$, i.e.\ specifying
\[ P(Y_1, \dots, Y_n) \]
for any $n$ and any $t_1, \dots, t_n$.

Given the model, the \textbf{predictive distribution} is
\[ p(y_{t+1} \mid y_{1:t}). \]
From this we can compute summaries: $E(Y_{t+1}\mid y_{1:t})$, $\mathrm{Var}(Y_{t+1}\mid y_{1:t})$, intervals, etc.

trash.title: Markov chain — definition
Transition matrix P
trash.content:
\textbf{\textcolor{red}{TRANSITION MATRIX}}

Finite state space $\mathcal{Y} = \{1, 2, \dots, N\}$. The transition probabilities at time $t$ are\[ p^{(t)}_{i,j} = P(Y_t = j \mid Y_{t-1} = i), \qquad i, j \in \mathcal{Y}. \]Arrange them in a matrix $\mathbf{P}^{(t)}$ with \emph{rows} indexed by the state at $t-1$ and \emph{columns} indexed by the state at $t$:

\begin{tabular}{|c|c|c|c|c|}
\hline
$t - 1 \;\backslash\; t$ & $1$ & $2$ & $\cdots$ & $N$ \\
\hline
$1$ & $p^{(t)}_{1,1}$ & $p^{(t)}_{1,2}$ & $\cdots$ & $p^{(t)}_{1,N}$ \\
$2$ & $p^{(t)}_{2,1}$ & $p^{(t)}_{2,2}$ & $\cdots$ & $p^{(t)}_{2,N}$ \\
$\vdots$ & $\vdots$ & $\vdots$ & $\ddots$ & $\vdots$ \\
$N$ & $p^{(t)}_{N,1}$ & $p^{(t)}_{N,2}$ & $\cdots$ & $p^{(t)}_{N,N}$ \\
\hline
\end{tabular}

\textbf{Row-stochastic:} each row sums to 1, $\sum_{j=1}^{N} p^{(t)}_{i,j} = 1$ for every $i$ and every $t$ — given that you are in state $i$ at $t-1$, you must end up \emph{somewhere} at time $t$.

\textbf{Homogeneous case.} If the transition probabilities do not depend on $t$, i.e.\ $p^{(t)}_{i,j} = p_{i,j}$ for every $t$, then the chain is \textbf{homogeneous}. The superscript drops:\[ \mathbf{P}^{(t)} \equiv \mathbf{P} = \big(p_{i,j}\big)_{i,j \in \mathcal{Y}}, \]a single $N \times N$ matrix that — together with the initial distribution $p_0(\cdot)$ — fully specifies the law of the chain.
